A review on turbulent flow over rough surfaces: Fundamentals and theories

Highlights

  • •
    Townsend hypothesis can explain large-scale motions near rough and smooth walls.
  • •
    Is unable to describe all roughness regimes and does not scale d-type roughness.
  • •
    Wall similarity hypothesis faces both supporting and conflicting evidence.
  • •
    Roughness function can be scaled with height and effective slope of roughness.
  • •
    Available models do not point to agreed conclusions or trends for all roughness types,

Abstract

Surface roughness can significantly influence the fluid dynamics and heat transfer in convective flows by inducing perturbations in the velocity profile which affect surface drag, turbulent mixing and heat transfer. While surface roughness can often negatively affect the performance of systems, it can also lead to performance improvements, such as in convective flows where roughness elements have been shown to enhance heat transfer. Turbulent flows over rough surfaces have been studied for about a century leading to significant developments in this field. Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) has made significant contributions to the knowledge of turbulent flows over rough surfaces as well as evaluation of the developed theories. Moreover, the turbulent closures model has seen wide use for simulation of rough-wall turbulent flows in practical applications where DNS is hindered by its complexity and computational resources.
Despite a significant number of experimental and CFD studies and the latest advances in this field, a recent review was not available. Therefore, this review surveys the past and recent experimental and numerical studies to address the fundamentals and theories related to the structure of turbulent flows over rough walls. This study chiefly investigates the structure of mean flow profile over rough surfaces, and its correlation with smooth wall mean flow profile. This review study can contribute to prospective experimental and CFD work, and for characterising rough-wall turbulent flows and heat transfer in different academic and engineering applications such as aerodynamics, hydraulics, meteorology, and manufacturing.
The review concludes that despite significant progress, the structure of turbulent flow is still not fully understood. This is mainly due to a lack of systematic studies on the structure of turbulent flow and also due to the variety of roughness which influence the dynamics of the flow in the roughness sublayers. The current roughness scale (sand-grain roughness height) fails to completely characterise roughness in many cases. Therefore, there is a need for a universal roughness scale that can describe every type of roughness and be used in any rough-flow regimes, including fully rough and transitionally rough regimes.

1. Introduction

The study of roughness in turbulent flows was pioneered by Hagen [1] and Darcy [2] who found that roughness affected pressure drop by increasing the drag force and blockage effects [3]. The formation of the boundary layer over surfaces significantly influences transport phenomena such as heat and momentum transfer. The roughness of these surfaces can significantly affect the boundary layer flow and thus influence heat and momentum transfer over the fluid-surface interface. Fig. 1 illustrates the boundary layer profile over smooth and rough surfaces. At the leading edge of the plate, flow is laminar; until at some point flow instability occurs initiating a laminar-turbulent transition.
For a turbulent boundary layer over a smooth surface, a thin layer of laminar flow known as the viscous sublayer forms along the entire length of the surface, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). For the same flow over a rough surface Fig. 1 (b), the roughness increases flow instability close to the wall which can lead to increased localised turbulence disrupting the viscous sublayer, thereby generating the roughness sublayer and affecting pressure drop and heat transfer.
Surface roughness may be a result of the manufacturing processes [4] and the normal use of a product (wear and tear). It may also result from mechanisms – including erosion, corrosion and deposition processes such as in gas turbines [5,6], ice accretion on aircraft wings [7], [8], [9], deposit in combustion chambers [10], and biofouling on ship hulls and marine machinery [11,12]. These types of roughness can compromise the safety, performance, and efficiency of systems, mainly due to the change in the turbulent structure as well as momentum and energy transfer. For example, in a review study on gas turbines, Bons [5], reported that natural degradation and deposition processes affected the surface roughness enough to reduce the performance of both compressor and turbine.
“Atmospheric Boundary Layer” (ABL) flows is another area, where flow over terrain, plant and urban canopies (Fig. 2 (a)) act as roughness which influences meteorological and local climate predictions [16], [17], [18], [19], [20]. Relevant reviews in ABL include Raupach et al. [21] on theoretical and experimental studies of turbulent flow boundary layers, Raupach & Tom [22] and Finnigan [17] on flow studies over plant canopies, and Roth [23] and Barlow and Coceal [24] on ABL over cities. Although they are occasionally compared with the high Reynolds number limit of industrial rough-wall turbulent flows, the study of geophysical flow is beyond the scope of this review paper.
Intentionally manufactured roughness features are employed for drag reduction and aerodynamic performance improvement [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30] as well as heat transfer enhancement [30], [31], [32], [33]. Dimples on golf balls [34,35], sharkskin denticles on aircraft surfaces [25,36] provide drag reduction, while heat transfer enhancement in roughened solar air heaters was reported by Sharma and Kalamkar [37], Gawande et al. [38], and Alam and Kim [39]. Roughness can improve the wettability of the surface hydrophobicity [40,41] as well as repellency of the hydrophilic surfaces [42]; which in turn, significantly influence the performance of many fluid flow devices such as heat pipes [43,44], desalination system [45], [46], [47], etc.
Surface roughness can also be incorporated with other heat transfer enhancement methods such as modified fluids, especially those containing nano-particles. These “nanofluids” have been found to further improve the performance of the heat exchangers [48,49] and as a new generation of heat transfer fluids, have shown great promise in heat transfer enhancement [50,51]. It has been proved that geometrical constraints such as surface roughness can influence the thermal performance of nanofluids including via increased area and eddy effects [51], [52], [53].
Recent advances in manufacturing, including Additive Manufacturing (AM), permit the fabrication of engineered rough surfaces as a design parameter, allowing more control of the shape and pattern of the roughness elements that may be difficult to produce by traditional methods [54,55]. The application of AM in the fabrication of thermal management systems and aerospace applications has rapidly increased in recent years and is an active research topic. AM processes can leave irregular and random surface roughness, the measurement of which were reviewed by Townsend [56]. Other researchers [57], [58], [59], [60] have studied the effects of AM fabricated rough surfaces on fluid flow and heat transfer.
As well as experimental studies, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has been widely adopted for rough flow studies. Surface roughness can be accounted for in CFD by either including roughness effects in turbulent CFD models, such as wall-modelled LES or Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS), or direct resolving via using DNS or LES. The adoption of a suitable numerical method depends on the physics of the problem (Geometry, Reynolds number, etc.) and more importantly, the available computational resources. Modern computing capabilities have enabled researchers to perform Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of turbulent flows over rough surfaces with complex geometries, including irregular/random roughness [61], [62], [63], [64], [65], [66], [67], [68], [69] or scanned real surfaces [10,[70], [71], [72], [73], [74], [75]].
Several textbooks include information on flow and heat transfer over surface roughness such as by Schlichting [76], Wilcox [77] and Kays and Crowford [78]. Despite a large number of experimental and CFD studies on the effect of surface roughness on flow and heat transfer, the number of comprehensive review papers related to this subject is surprisingly low, and most of them were published decades ago. In 1985, Patel et al. [79] reviewed turbulent models for near-wall, and low Reynolds number flows with a small emphasis on surface roughness. Subsequently, in 1991, Raupach et al. [21] reviewed the experimental and theoretical findings of both laboratory and experimental studies on ABL flows. In 1998, Patel [80] reviewed the studies on high Reynolds number flows over rough surfaces for prospective CFD applications. He presented the strength and weakness of some CFD turbulent models for flow over rough surfaces and asserted the need for further experimental studies and more accurate numerical methods for flow over surface roughness. In 2004, Jiménez [81] surveyed the experimental studies related to the characterisation of turbulent flows over different type of roughness. In 2010, Bons reviewed the past 60 years of studies on the effects of surface roughness on gas turbine performance. In the same year, Flack and Schultz [82] surveyed predictive methods used to determine the frictional drag on rough surfaces. More recently, in 2019, Piomelli [83] gave a review of the studies conducted with DNS and LES at the Turbulence Simulation and Modelling Laboratory at Queen's University, Canada, emphasizing the usefulness of the data that can be achieved by numerical simulation while espousing the need for a more complete research review on this subject.
From the above survey, a wide gap exists for a comprehensive review of recent and past experimental and numerical studies on the fundamentals and theories of rough-wall turbulent flows. Therefore, this paper provides an overview of past and recent studies in this field in the following structure.
This study chiefly focuses on the difference between the mean flow profile over smooth and rough surfaces; thus, sections are structured as follows. First, a brief background of surface roughness effects on fluid dynamics and heat transfer in large- to nano-scale rough-wall flows is given. A brief review on mean turbulent flow over smooth walls and related theories and their extension to rough-wall flows are presented, including the validity of Townsend's wall similarity hypothesis. This is followed by discussions on the characterisation of roughness and rough-wall flows, comprising a review on d-type and k-type roughness. Subsequently, approaches for the characterisation of rough flow regimes and related correlations are reviewed. The mean flow over rough surfaces as well as the effect of surface roughness on fluid flow and heat transfer are then discussed.
Finally, this review study can contribute to prospective experimental and CFD research, and for characterising rough-wall turbulent flows that are relevant to broad range of academic and engineering applications such as aerodynamics, hydraulics, meteorology, manufacturing etc.
Hereafter, in this study, the velocity field V = u(u, v, w) has the components of u,  v and w for the streamwise (x), normal-wall (y), and spanwise (z) directions respectively with the mean velocity being represented by U. Any quantity with the superscript “+” denotes the dimensionless wall quantities (for example U+ = U/U* and y+ = yU*/ν), where ν is the fluid viscosity. The friction velocity is also defined as U*=τw/ρ with τw the wall shear stress and ρ the fluid density. Note that the friction velocity is also referred to as “wall friction velocity”, “shear velocity”, or “wall shear velocity”. The thickness of the boundary layer is represented by δ while k, ks, ks+=ksU*/ν represent the roughness height, equivalent sand-grain roughness height (see Section 4.1), and roughness Reynolds number (see Section 4.2), respectively.

2. Structure of wall-bounded turbulent flows

2.1. Mean flow over smooth walls

Turbulent flows are irregular in nature, and the variations from one instant to another is substantial; however, the bulk flow can be described by mean flow characteristics. Any expressions and law for the description of the mean flow must, not only express the mean flow pattern but also satisfy the non-slip boundary condition at the wall and the condition of the zero-slope of velocity at the edge of the boundary layer. The bulk properties of mean flow in both smooth- and rough-wall boundary layers can be derived by classical asymptotic matching process [21,84,85]. Let δ be the thickness of boundary layer and u* the friction velocity (τw/ρ) (with τw the wall shear stress and ρ the fluid density). Assume also the flow is in the “equilibrium” state, in which δ and u* have a sufficient slow variation in the streamwise direction x. Therefore, both δ and u* can be considered as local scale at any particular x direction. The asymptotic matching analysis suggests that the boundary layer (over both smooth and rough walls) comprises of two overlapping regions; an outer layer scaling with u* and δ, and an inner layer scaling with u* and a set of length scales characterising the surface. For smooth surfaces, the set of length scales includes just the viscous length scale ν/u*, while, for rough surfaces, it consists of ν/u* in addition to all length scales required to completely characterise the roughness (e.g. roughness height, kurtosis, skewness, etc.).
The damping effect of the wall alters the regime of the turbulent flow close to the wall and leads to the formation of the boundary layer flow over the wall into several distinct layers. Fig. 3 illustrates the variation of the dimensionless mean velocity profile of the turbulent boundary layer with the logarithmic distance from the wall. The turbulent boundary layer consists of an “inner layer” which is attached to the wall and the “outer layer” that is generated above the inner layer. The inner layer is associated with the active region of turbulent flow that is affected by viscosity and local flow parameters. In contrast, the outer layer is associated with the inactive turbulent region that is influenced by the wall geometry. The inner region itself consists of three subsequence layers: “viscous (laminar) sublayer”, “buffer layer”, and “logarithmic layer”.
In the viscous (laminar) sublayer, which is attached to the surface, the mean velocity can be expressed as [86](1)U+=y+;
The aptly named log-layer region comprises a natural logarithmic velocity distribution, which is referred to as the “law of the wall” (also termed as “log-law”) and expressed as:(2)U+=1κln(y+)+C,where κ is the von Karman constant (κ ≈ 0.41), and the value of constant C is approximately 5.1. The log-layer is a fully turbulent layer in which the Reynolds shear stress greatly exceeds the viscous shear stress. There is a transition layer, known as the “buffer layer” between viscous sublayer and log layer where viscous shear stress almost equals the Reynolds shear stress (−ρu′v′¯). The buffer layer is characterised by a high-level turbulent mixing due to turbulent production in this region and increased turbulence intensity. The log-layer region is also characterised by turbulence intensity and production, but to a lesser degree, since it has a smaller velocity gradient compared to the buffer layer.
The logarithmic law is not applicable in the outer layer (y+ > 700) since the measured turbulent velocity exceeds the predicted values. The outer layer is unaffected by the direct influence of the wall, which extended to 70% or 80% of the total thickness of the boundary layer. In this region, free shear layer prevails, and the velocity profile deviates considerably from the logarithmic form. The outer layer is also called the defect layer because there is some apparent velocity defect with respect to the free-stream velocity.
In order to cover the defect layer, Coles [90] suggested that the standard velocity profile of a turbulent boundary layer, with the linear and logarithmic sublayer, could be modified with an additional wake function that comes into effect gradually as the outer edge of the boundary layer approaches. The Coles’ “law-of-the-wake” is written as(3)U+=1κln(y+)+C+Π(x)κω(yδ).
Coles’ “law-of-the-wake” is a superposition of the law-of-the-wall due to the wall shear stress and the law of the wake due to the free turbulence at the core. Wake functions ω identify how wake modification emerges with increasing y. Coles [90] expressed the wake function numerically, and [91] approximated it as a sine-squared function.(4)ω(yδ)=2Πκ(sinπ.y2δ)2.
The Π function represents the free turbulence effect on the mean velocity, which may vary along the streamwise direction x. The Π function depends on the pressure gradient and describes how retarded the boundary layer is and how well-developed the wake region is. Usually, the wake function is normalized such that ω(1) = 2, and thus the Π function characterizes the strength of the wake in terms of the deviation from the log law at y = δ [92,93]. Chauhan et al. [92] suggested a composite profile fit comprising exponential functions that enable calculations of δ and Π for boundary layer. The adapted versions of these profiles were employed by Nagib & Chauhan [94] for pipe and channel flows. An alternative versions of the law-of-the-wake have been proposed by several researchers [95], [96], [97], [98], [99], [100], [101], [102], [103], [104].
The simple law-of-the-wall (the log-law) does not satisfy the no-slip boundary condition at the wall and the condition of zero-slope of the velocity profile at the outer edge of the boundary layer. The law-of-the-wake also does not satisfy the no-slip boundary condition. Spalding [105] proposed a single equation that covers all four layers (viscous, buffer, log law, and defect layers) and has reported excellent agreement with experimental data in the range of 0 ≤ y+ ≤ 2000 [106,107]. The Spalding law-of-the-wall is expressed as(5)y+=U++exp(−κc)[exp(κU+)−1−∑n=14(κU+)nn!]for0≤y+≤2000.where the recommended values for κ and c are 0.4 and 5.5, respectively.
Reichardt [108] suggested a correlation for the mean velocity profile of based on the turbulent flow data in pipe and channels, which represent the velocity distribution close to the wall as well as in the core of flow, expressed as(6)U+=1κln(1+κy+)+7.8[1−exp(−y+11)−(y+11)exp(−0.33y+)]
The Spalding law and Reichardt law can be applied to predict incompressible turbulent flow without adverse pressure gradient and separation. Moreover, both of them satisfy the no-slip condition; however, the zero slope of velocity profile at the outer edge of the boundary layer is not fulfilled, as shown in Fig. 3. Kestin and Richardson [109] summarise the mean velocity profile in the inner region of the turbulent boundary layer.
Turbulent heat transfer over smooth surfaces can be determined by the Reynolds analogy. Based on the similarity between hydraulic and thermal boundary layer, Reynolds [110] postulates the existence of an analogy between wall shear stress, τw,and heat flux, qw. More discussion on the Reynolds analogy and temperature profile over smooth walls can be found in Bejan [111] and Kays and Crawford [78].
Several hypotheses have been developed to explain the structure of the turbulent boundary layer. Ludwig Prandtl hypothesised the first theory in this field, which is referred to as Prandtl's mixing length theory [113]. The mixing length theory states that the horizontal component of mean flow is proportional to the logarithm of height. Prandtl's mixing length theory assumes that the fluid fluctuations can be simplified and displaced by a distance l, known as Prandtl's mixing length, perpendicular to the main flow direction. Accordingly, the turbulence model of the mixing length can be described by the following equation [76](7)τt=ρℓ2|∂U∂y|∂U∂y,where τt is turbulent shear stress which is a model of the shear stress created by turbulent fluctuations. Subsequent to Prandtl's mixing length theory, two important hypotheses, the Monin–Obukhov (M-O) similarity hypothesis, and Townsend hypothesis were developed and are now discussed in the following sections.

2.2. Monin–Obukhov (M-O) similarity

The M-O Similarity was originally proposed based on the important understanding of Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) flows. This hypothesis describes the atmospheric boundary layer by Monin–Obukhov (also referred as to Obukhov) length scale, L, expressed as [114], [115], [116], [117], [118], [119](8)L=−(U*)3κ(gTw)(qρcp),where κ is the von Karman constant and U* is friction velocity and g is gravity acceleration, while Tw, q,  ρ, and cp are the wall temperature, kinematic heat flux, fluid density, and fluid heat capacity, respectively. M-O similarity stated that the local variable of turbulent flow could be characterised by “universal functions”. In accordance with the Monin–Obukhov dimensionless parameter ξ = y/L (where y is the direction normal to the surface), the velocity and temperature profile can be expressed as [120,121]:(9)(κyU*)∂U∂y=φm(ξ);(10)(yTw)∂T∂y=φH(ξ);where U and T are mean velocity and mean temperature profiles, respectively, while ϕm and ϕH are momentum and heat exchange universal functions, respectively. Based on experimental observations, several universal functions have been developed in the literature [122], [123], [124], [125], [126], [127], [128], [129]. More discussions on the universal functions can be found in Maronga and Reuder [130], Blaunshtein and Kopeika [121], and Foken [120]. Fig. 4 compares some of the universal functions reported in distinctive studies in the literature and demonstrates that universal functions proposed by different authors are in agreement for ξ <  0 (unstable flow stratification condition) but not for ξ >  0 (stable flow stratification conditions).
Nosov et al. [133], Markowski et al. [134], Guo and Zuo [135], and Blaunshtein and Kopeika [121] presented some of the recent experiments in this field. Although M-O similarity is universally accepted, despite the validation by field experiments and recent theoretical justifications of the M-O universal functions [136], [137], [138], [139], [140], the universality of similarity functions is questionable [141]. In the literature, numerical studies of the validity of the M-O similarity have been performed using LES [130,[142], [143], [144], [145], [146]] and DNS [144,[147], [148], [149], [150], [151], [152], [153]]. Many of these studies calculated universal functions and compared them with predicted ones in the literature, and demonstrated a large scatter for ϕm compared to that of ϕH.
Foken [129] reviewed the history, experiments, and findings related to M-O similarity. He reported that this theory (even under ideal conditions) has an accuracy of only about 10-20% (typically associated with the universal functions). He also mentioned that M-O similarity is valid mostly within the surface layer, where the turbulent fluxes do not vary more than approximately 10 % of their surface value. McNaughton and Brunet [141] stated that M-O similarity's failure is due to its incomplete basis of parameters since the Monin–Obukhov length scale itself depends on the free stream flow parameters. The M-O similarity is limited to the surface layer and above the roughness sublayer (see Fig. 2 (a)) and probably is not valid for large roughness [129,131]. Recently, Yang et al. [154] reported that the M-O similarity provides good predictions of the mean flow characteristics; however, its evaluation of the turbulent fluctuations is far from satisfactory. Tong and Nguyen [155] showed that the incomplete similarity is related to two assumptions used in M-O similarity: (i) the length scale of the energy-containing eddies only scales with y, and (2) L is only a vertical length scale. Multi-point Monin–Obukhov similarity (MMO similarity) was proposed to address the incomplete similarity in the M-O hypothesis [155], [156], [157], [158]. More information on MMO similarity can be found elsewhere [155], [156], [157], [158], [159].
M-O similarity has received significant attention for predicting the ABL, especially in most state-of-the-art LES models. It issued as a surface boundary condition to calculate the surface Reynolds stress and the turbulent surface sensible and latent heat fluxes, for example, see Ref. [160], [161], [162]. A wide range of studies has employed M-O similarity for considering the effect of the surface roughness in LES (for example, see Ref. [163], [164], [165], [166], [167]). Several researchers have pointed out that M-O similarity can only be considered valid within the internal layer (see Fig. 2 (a)) and the upper part of the surface layer; however, it fails in the roughness sublayer (see Fig. 2 (a)), where the direct effect of the roughness elements are presented [168], [169], [170], [171], [172]. For an unstable condition, the height of internal sublayer y* (top of the roughness sublayer) is corresponded to y* = 35y0, where y0 is the hydrodynamic roughness length [168]. However, Physick and Garratt [170] suggested y* = 50y0 and noted that value of y* might be smaller for stable condition. Garratt [168] and Harman and Finnigan [171] suggested universal functions for below y* so as to accommodate the roughness sublayer. Based on the previous studies, Basu and Lacser [172] suggested employing y* = 50y0 as a general rule for LES models, which also used in wall-modelled LES by Maronga et al. [166]. Recently Couvreux et al. [165] analysed the results of ten LES codes and reported a substantial sensitivity of surface fluxes to the specified hydrodynamic roughness length.

2.3. Townsend hypothesis

Despite these shortcomings, the M-O similarity implies that flow can be divided into two separate regions that seem to not interact with each other. This observation, as well as observations indicated by Townsend [222] and Bradshaw [223], led to the development of Townsend hypothesis that has been widely employed to describe turbulent flow over smooth and rough surfaces. Based on Townsend [173] and Bradshaw [174] observations in the laboratory boundary layer, Bradshaw [175] suggested that large-scale motions near smooth walls have no noticeable influence on the relation between shear stress and velocity profile near the wall. Townsend [173] proposed a general hypothesis that the near-wall turbulent flow can be divided into two turbulent regions: “active” and “inactive” regions. The former region is involved in momentum transfer while the latter is not, and these two turbulent regions do not interact. Active turbulence is generated by shear force and scales on the local parameters of the flow and is responsible for producing the Reynolds shear stress. On the other hand, inactive turbulence is produced by the high energy process far from the surface and scales on outer layer parameters. Townsend hypothesis implies that the inertial turbulent scales (also termed the energy-containing motions) dominate the active region and beyond are large relative to the viscous length scale. The inertial scales are independent of Reynolds number since the upper part of the active region is a fixed fraction of the boundary layer thickness, typically 0.15 δ.
Townsend [176] described a conceptual model through which the kinematics of boundary layer flow can be statistically explained by the hierarchy of geometrically self-similar attached momentum-carrying motions (or eddies) that are randomly distributed in the flow field and internally dominated. Townsend expressed his Attached Eddy Hypothesis (AEH) as:
“The velocity fields of the main eddies, regarded as persistent, organised flow patterns, extend to the wall and, in a sense, they are attached to the wall.” (Townsend [176], p. 153)
AEH explains that the dominant energy-containing motions in the turbulent boundary layer are due to large eddies attached to the wall. These attached eddies have a population density inversely proportional to their height ranging from a height of O(y) to a height of O(δ). He proposed using the self-similar function, s1, to model the velocity field V = (u, v, w) for an eddy centred at (xa,ya,za) and superimposed on a uniform background flow as(11)V=(u,v,w)=s1[(x−xa)ya+(y−ya)ya+(z−za)ya].
Several studies have completed the original picture by Townsend [177], [178], [179], [180], while plenty of studies have supported the existence of attached eddies in wall-bounded turbulent flows [181], [182], [183], [184], [185], [186], [187], [188], [189], [190], [191], [192]. Further discussion on self-similar and attached eddies can be found in McKeon [181]. In a further development on AEH, the Attached Eddy Model (AEM) [193,194] was developed based on Townsend's attached eddy hypothesis [176]. The AEM has proven to provide an effective method for predicting velocity statistics as well as a framework for interpreting the energy-containing flow physics at high Reynolds numbers [194]. The AEM permitted Townsend [176] to make predictions of dimensionless quadrant-decomposed Reynolds shear stress in the active region as(12a)u′2¯+=B1−A1lnyδ,(12b)v′2¯+=B3(12c)w′2¯+=B2−A2lnyδ,(12d)u′v′¯+=B4where A1, A2, B1 B2, B3, and B4 are constants. AEH suggests a logarithmic law to characterizes streamwise and spanwise turbulence intensity in the inertial region. Several experiments at high Reynolds number [195], [196], [197], [198], [199], [200], [201], [202], [203] and recent DNS studies [192,[204], [205], [206], [207]] have reported substantial support for the AEH formulation in Eq. (12a) (a-d). More discussions on the velocity components and turbulent statistics in active and inactive regions can be found elsewhere [208].
A few studies have demonstrated similar logarithmic scaling for higher moments of u′ [209] and w′ [210,211]. The validity of logarithmic decay of the statistical moments with respect to y has been verified by numerous studies [198,200,204,206,209,212,213]. Among all, Hultmark et al. [214] measured the logarithmic scaling of streamwise turbulence intensity in pipe flows at high Reynolds numbers. Yamamoto & Tsuji [212] performed DNS of high Reynolds number turbulent channel flows and showed logarithmic scaling of streamwise turbulence intensity. The active and inactive region can be deemed uncorrelated only if the nonlinear interaction across these motions are ignored, which have been observed to exist [215], [216], [217], [218], [219]. However, such interaction will not significantly influence the Reynolds stress and turbulent statistics [208]. More information on AEM can be found in a comprehensive review by Marusic and Monty [194].

2.4. Wall similarity hypothesis

In order to develop engineering models for the turbulent boundary layer over rough surfaces, knowledge of the structure of these type of flows is required. Current engineering models consider the influence of roughness as small perturbations to the smooth wall boundary layer [80]. Therefore, most of the rough-wall turbulent models have been developed based on the extension of smooth-wall turbulent flow data to the rough-walls. The “wall similarity hypothesis” is an extension to Townsend's Reynolds number similarity hypothesis [176]. Townsend thoroughly described the general structure of turbulent flows in his book [176], by which he explained his hypothesis and also postulated the Reynolds number similarity expressed as:
“while geometrically similar flows are expected to be dynamically similar if their Reynolds numbers are the same, their structures are also very nearly similar for all Reynolds numbers which are large enough to allow (fully) turbulent flow.” (Townsend [176], p. 53)
Based on Townsend's Reynolds number similarity, the wall similarity hypothesis for turbulent flow over both rough and smooth surfaces as
“outside the roughness (or viscous) sublayer, the turbulent motion in a boundary layer at high Reynolds number are independent of the wall roughness and the viscosity, except for the role of the wall in setting velocity scale U*, the height Y = y − d and the boundary layer thickness δ.”
Here, d is the zero-plane displacement. The wall similarity hypothesis is also referred to in the literature as the Townsend Reynolds similarity for rough-walls. Wall similarity was supported with the scaling law for velocity spectra in several overlapping spectral ranges by Perry and Abell [220] and also by Perry and Chong [193] and Perry et al. [221,222]. This hypothesis was later labelled as “wall similarity” by Raupach et al. [21]. The wall similarity hypothesis is also referred to as the outer-layer similarity in the literature.
According to the wall similarity, for sufficiently high Reynolds numbers outside the viscous sublayer, the turbulent motions are independent of surface conditions and viscosity (except for wall shear stress and the boundary layer thickness). This means that the turbulent stress, normalised by the wall shear stress, is universal outside the roughness sublayer. The outer region has been generally thought to be unaffected by roughness, as reported in reviews by Raupach et al. [21] and Jiménez [81]. This implies that the mean flow for both smooth and rough walls obeys the universal velocity defect law in the overlap and outer region of the boundary layer, which is expressed as [21]:(13)Ue+−U+=f(yδ)
Fig. 5 illustrates the defect velocity of zero pressure gradient turbulent flow over different roughness. In Fig. 5, Reθ is the friction Reynolds number that represents the Reynolds number based on the friction velocity Mean flow similarity can be observed through the overlapping of smooth and rough wall data when plotted in a velocity-defect form.
The wall similarity hypothesis (universal velocity defect law) has been supported by numerous studies with different types of roughness [224,[226], [227], [228], [229], [230], [231], [232], [233], [234], [235], [236], [237], [238], [239], [240]]. The validity of wall similarity hypothesis and defect velocity law has also been verified by numerous experimental studies performed by Karen A. Flack and Michae P. Schultz and their colleagues [82,223,[235], [236], [237],[241], [242], [243], [244], [245], [246], [247], [248], [249], [250], [251]] and also Kenneth T. Christensen and his colleagues [87,224,225,[252], [253], [254], [255], [256], [257]]. Flack and Schultz [250] outline their 15 years of experimental research on rough-wall turbulent flows, where they reported the observation of wall similarity hypothesis in all their experiments. They also demonstrated that similarity in the outer layer is also observed in the quadrant-decomposed components of Reynolds stress (u′2¯+,v′2¯+) and in the turbulent transport of the Reynolds stress (−u′v′¯+). Apart from experimental studies, wall similarity has been validated with DNS of turbulent flow over rough surfaces; including the recent studies of Busse et al. [71], Thakkar at al. [72,73], Busse and Jelly [258], Jayaraman and Khan [259], and Khan and Jayaraman [260].
Some researchers have observed exceptions to wall similarity and outer layer sensitivity to surface condition. These exceptions to wall similarity mostly observed in two-dimensional roughness elements, although recent studies have indicated the validity of wall similarity for two-dimensional roughness [250]. The studies of turbulent flows over woven meshes by Krogstad et al. [261] and transverse bars by Keirsbulck et al. [262] indicated an increase in the wake strength of the mean velocity profile. Krogstad and Antonia [263] reported alterations in the turbulent structure in the outer layer for a woven mesh roughness. Krogstad and Antonia [264] observed variations in the Reynolds shear stress profiles for surface covered with transverse rods. Schultz et al. [265] indicated that wall effects could have a larger influence on the outer flow with a roughly 40% extension of the attached eddies into the boundary layer, for 2D roughness. Some of the recent DNS studies have also reported a poor match between the smooth and rough wall data in the outer region such as DNS of turbulent flow over streamwise-aligned triangular ridges by Stroh et al. [266]. Lee and Sung [267] performed DNS study of turbulent flows over transverse squared rods [266]. They showed self-preservation of defect velocity can be achieved at about x > 300δin, where x is the streamwise direction and δin is the thickness of the boundary layer at the inlet. Chung et al. [268] performed an idealised DNS study to evaluate the wall similarity hypothesis by comparing the effect of no-slip versus sheer stress boundary conditions and found that the outer flow is highly insensitive to the imposed wall boundary condition.
Flack et al. [235] outlined the exceptions to wall similarity and explained that these disparate findings are most likely due to “strong” roughness (as they termed) used in the studies. They defined strong roughness as roughness whose equivalent sand-grain roughness height ks is a significant portion of the inner layer thickness. This argument was also supported in the review by Jiménez [81] which stated that rough-wall flows with δ/k ≤ 40 may exhibit roughness effect well into the outer layer due to the destruction of a significant portion of the log-law region by roughness elements. An alternative criterion was reported by Flack et al. [235] as δ/ks < 40. The woven mesh, traverse rods, and transverse bars used in the studies of Krogstad et al. [261], Krogstad and Antonia [263], Keirsbulck et al. [262], and Stroh et al. [266] corresponds to δ/ks ≈ 15, δ/ks ≈ 8 δ/ks ≈ 7, and δ/k ≈ 6.5 respectively. Reynolds stresses of flow over distinctive rough surfaces agree well throughout most of the boundary layer and the wall similarity is maintained well outside of 3ks while the differences in higher moment turbulence statistics of different rough-wall boundary layers are confined to y < 5ks, as reported by Flack et al. [235].
Conflicting evidence has also been reported in the literature. In a review study, Flack and Schultz [250] evaluated the similarity hypothesis based on the data of several studies with a range of roughness from where similarity is expected to hold (δ/k = 110) to significantly rougher surfaces (δ/k = 16). They showed excellent agreement between smooth- and rough-wall profiles, indicating similarity in the mean flow. Mean flow similarity for large roughness was also supported by Castro [231] who showed similarity for δ/k > 5 and Wu and Christensen [224] who showed mean flow similarity for (δ/k = 27). Wu and Christensen [252] also observed that the quadrant-decomposed Reynolds shear stress and the Reynolds stress for smooth- and rough-wall cases with δ/k > 5 are in accordance with wall similarity hypothesis.

3. Surface roughness parameters and characterisation

This section briefly discusses surface roughness and the methods for characterisation of roughness from an engineering viewpoint. Generally, the surface texture, also known as surface finish and surface morphology, comprises a series of geometrical irregularities that are randomly or uniformly extended over a smooth surface [269]. The frequency of the height of irregularities quantifies the type of surface, as shown in Fig. 6. Geometrical irregularities with a high frequency are considered as “Roughness” while irregularities with a medium frequency are regarded as “Waviness”. Geometrical irregularities with a low frequency are known as “surface form” which is no longer considered as surface texture. The distinction between roughness, waviness and form can be found in Raja et al. [270].
Napoli et al. [61] introduced Effective Slope (ES) to distinguish between roughness and waviness surface, written as(14)ES=1lxlz∫0l∫0lz|∂k(x,z)∂x|dxdz.where k(x, z) is the roughness amplitude, which is also referred to as height map or height function, while lx and lz are sampling length in streamwise and spanwise directions, respectively. ES is defined as the average value of the magnitude of the slope of the roughness corrugation. Pyramid roughness and 2D wave-composite surfaces with an effective slope of approximately less than, 0.35, do not scale on the roughness height and are classified as wavy surfaces [61,249]. Yuan and Piomelli [64] found that the critical ES value for real rough surfaces is much larger than 0.35. Forooghi et al. [66] showed that, at lower values of the ES (mild slope), the surface slope becomes the main controlling factor and supresses the impact of the topographical parameters.

3.1. Roughness parameters

The flow characteristics over rough surfaces should be expressed in terms of statistical surface properties in order to be compatible with the stochastic nature of irregular roughness distribution. International standards have adopted numerous statistical surface parameters for the characterisation of surface roughness [271,272]. Examples of these standards are ASME Y14.36M and ISO 1302. A roughness parameter can be calculated either on a profile of a sampling line l (Fig. 7) or on a sampling area A. The parameters defined based on the profile of the sampling length (known as R parameters) are more common while those identified based on the sampling area (known as S parameters) give more significant values.
Amplitude parameters (R or S) can be defined using a heightmap used to characterize the surface based on the vertical deviations of the roughness profile from the mean line. Commonly-used amplitude parameters (based on the profile shown in Fig. 7) are listed in Table 1 [272]. The roughness amplitude y must be centred, meaning that the mean height calculated on the sampling length l is already subtracted from the heights [190] and n is the number of measured points on the surface

Table 1. Definition of roughness parameters.

ParameterDescriptionMathematical descriptionDiscrete implementation
RaArithmetic mean deviation1l∫|y|dx1n∑i=1n|yi|
RqRoot-mean-square roughness1l∫|y|dx1n∑i=1nyi2
RvMaximum valley depth below the mean line, within a single sampling length|min y(x)||min yi|
RpMaximum peak height above the mean line, within a single sampling lengthmax y(x)max yi
RzMaximum peak to valley height of the profileRv + Rp
Rz(DIN)Ten-point height based on the definition in DIN standard, within a five sampling length110(∑j=15Rp,j+∑j=15Rv,j)
Rz(ISO)Ten-point height based on the definition in ISO standard, within a five sampling length15(∑j=15Rp,j−∑j=15Rv,j)
skskewness1(Rq)31l∫|y|3dx1n(Rq)3∑i=1nyi3
kukurtosis1(Rq)41l∫y4dx1n(Rq)4∑i=1nyi4
The Rq parameter statistically defines the standard deviation of the heights distribution on the surface and is of more physical significance than Ra. The sole use of the Ra parameter can lead to misinterpretation of the surface characteristics since different surface structures can possess the same Ra value. The Rz parameter is more sensitive to occasional high peaks or deep valleys than that of Ra.
The skewness is a measure of the profile symmetry and describes the shape of the topography height distribution and can be positive, negative or zero. This parameter is sensitive to occasional deep valleys or high peaks. For a surface with symmetrical topography, i.e. a surface with many peaks as valleys such as Gaussian surfaces, the skewness is zero. A surface with valleys filled in or high peaks (such as deposition on surface, porous, and sintered) has positive skewness. In contrast, surfaces with peaks removed or deep valleys (such as corrosion and scratched) possess a negative skewness. The schematic representation of three types of skewness is illustrated in Fig. 8 (a).
The kurtosis, ku, is a measure of the sharpness of the surface height distribution. The kurtosis characterises the distribution of the height and is strictly positive. If ku < 3, the distribution curve is referred to as Platykurtoic and has relatively few high peaks and low valleys. If ku > 3, the distribution curve is referred to as Leptokurtoic and has relatively many high peaks and low valleys. The schematic representation of three types of kurtosis is shown in Fig. 8 (b).

3.2. Characterisation of surface roughness

The characteristics of roughness can be sufficiently described with the utilisation of the Probability Distribution Function (PDF). It represents the probability of a point on the surface that has a height equal to y; thus it is given as [273]:(15)∫−∞+∞p(y)dy=1
The distribution curves shown in Fig. 8 are examples of the different possible shape of PDF. The shape of the PDF provides useful information about the surface's nature and can be evaluated by its moments. The central ϑth moment of the PDF with zero mean, mϑ, is defined as [273](16)mϑ=∫−∞+∞yϑp(y)dyorindescreteformmϑ=1n∑i=1nyiϑ
It can be seen that the first moment is zero. The first four moments can adequately describe any statistical distribution of roughness [64,82,224,249,252,274]. The various surface roughness parameters found in the literature can be mathematically determined by using PDF moments. As to the definitions of roughness parameters, described in Table 1, the roughness parameters can be defined as:(17)Rq=m2;Sk=m3/m23/2;ku=m4/m24
In the past few decades, the characterisation of the roughness scale in turbulent flows has been linked to the statistical moments of the surface PDF up to fourth-order [64,66,275,276]. Recent studies concerning rough-wall flows analysed by the statistical moments up to fourth-order can be found elsewhere [64,82,224,249,252,274].
According to Flack and Schultz [82], a single measure of roughness height, such as Ra or Rq, is not able to fully describe the surface roughness. They showed that the surface roughness could be characterized merely by root-mean-square roughness height and the skewness (or the kurtosis), which have also been supported by other studies [277,278]. Jelly and Busse [279] studied 174 skewness-kurtosis combinations of rough surfaces (natural or synthetic) taken from eleven independent surface measurements published in related literature. They demonstrated that most of the measured data is clustered around the Gaussian case, corresponding to sk = 0 and ku = 3.
Two more important parameters of surface roughness that can significantly influence the rough-wall flows are the solidity parameter λ and the shape parameter. The solidity parameter is defined as the ratio of the average roughness element spacing (ψ) to the effective slope roughness height (k), while the shape parameter is presented as the ratio of the frontal area of a single roughness element (Af) and the windward wetted surface area of the single roughness element (As) [280], [281], [282]. A relation of ES = 2λ has been observed by several researchers [3,61,72,268]. In a further attempt, Dirling [281] introduced a “combined solidity and shape parameter”, Λ, for 2D roughness, written as(18)Λ=(ψk)(AfAs)−4/3.
Sigal and Danberg [280] considered the effect of the roughness density for dense arrangements of two-dimensional transverse roughness including bars, rods, and ribs by including the reference surface area before the addition of roughness (S) and the total frontal area of the roughness (Sf), expressed as(19)Λs=(SSf)(AfAs)−1.6.
Since real-life roughness such as turbine blade roughness is random and highly non-uniform, some adoption is needed to apply the definition of Λs. For this reason, Bons [283] suggested dividing the surface into several cells and using a 3D surface topography point-by-point to measure the windward and wetted surface areas of each cell of the entire map. Thus, the Λs, modified can be obtained by modifying the definitions of parameters in Eq. (19) in such a way that S is equivalent to the platform area of the surface map and Sf becomes the summation of the windward projected area of each cell. Moreover, Af becomes the average windward projected area of all cells, while As is the average windward wetted area of all cells.

4. Characterisation of turbulent flow over rough surfaces

As explained in the introduction section, the surface roughness alters the characteristics of turbulent flows. The most significant effect of the wall roughness is increased drag and augmented wall-normal functions near the wall [261,284], which leads to a decrease in the anisotropy of the Reynolds stress [285]. Rough-wall turbulent flows were reviewed by Raupach at al. [21] and Jiménez [81]. They reported that that the boundary layer over both the smooth and rough walls possess quite different structures controlled by different length scales in the inner layer. However, away from the surface, the low-order statistics are reasonably similar, indicating that the outer layer is unaffected by the surface structure (whether it is smooth or rough). Despite long-term research, no universal method for estimation of friction losses has been developed so far; other than hydrodynamic tests or geometrically resolved DNS [286]. However, some empirical correlations for different types of roughness have been developed based on the experimental and DNS studies which are now reviewed in the following sections. [286].

4.1. Equivalent sand-grain roughness

In the derivation of log-law, it is assumed that the near-wall flow is characterised by the viscosity. However, this is merely true for hydrodynamically smooth surfaces where the average height of the surface roughness elements is less than the thickness of the viscous sublayer. Otherwise, the effect of the roughness on the flow should be considered by defining a roughness scale that reflects the effect of roughness characteristics on the flow. In the literature, the equivalent sand-grain roughness height is widely used for characterisation of roughness in rough-wall flows. The equivalent sand-grain approach stems from the pioneer works by Nikuradse [287,288] and Schlichting [3]. The origin of this approach dates from Nikuradse's sand-grain experiments which provided data on the scaling laws. The concept of this approach is based on the definition of a single length scale which can characterise the roughness. This length scale can be applied in various scaling laws for the velocity field and friction factors. Consider that the surface is covered with a layer of uniform packed spheres as dense as possible, as shown in Fig. 9 (a).
The diameter of the sphere is called sand-grain roughness height k for the sake of the similarity of the case with sandpaper. For the type of the surfaces physically similar to the sand-grain in Nikuradse's experiment, the length scale can be described by the sand-grain roughness height. However, when the shape of roughness deviates from the sand-grain, a single parameter cannot describe the sand-grain roughness anymore. In this case, geometrical parameters may be applied to characterise these type of surfaces [82]. Therefore, an equivalent length scale was introduced by Colebrook and White [289] referred to as a so-called equivalent sand-grain roughness ks, as shown in Fig. 9 (b). The equivalent sand-grain roughness is an equivalent roughness height for irregular, and non-uniform rough surfaces that produce the same results as the uniform sand-grain of the Nikuradse for a fully rough flow regime. The definition of the fully rough regime is presented in upcoming sections.

4.2. Rough flow regimes

The roughness modifies the law-of-the-wall used for the viscous sublayer. In the context of the law of the wall, the “roughness Reynolds number”ks+ is defined as(20)ks+=ksU*ν,
Corresponding to the three regions of the wall affected the turbulent boundary layer, the rough flow regimes can be classified into three main categories. Consider kSmooth+ and kRough+ as two critical limits of the roughness Reynolds number. Then, based on the different value for the roughness Reynolds number, three different roughness regimes, are defined as [287,288]
  • •
    Hydraulically smooth regime: If ks+≤kSmooth+, the roughness elements are entirely embedded in the viscous sublayer, as shown in Fig. 10 (a); thus, skin friction and drag coefficient are not modified.
  • •
    Transitionally rough regime: If kSmooth+≤ks+≤kRough+, the influence of the surface roughness is complex. In this regime, both the Reynolds number and relative roughness influence the skin friction and drag coefficients. This means that both viscous and pressure forces influence the skin friction and drag coefficient. The Transitionally rough regime is associated with the reduced sublayer thickness, as shown in Fig. 10 (b) – resulting in diminishing the influence of the wall damping effect.
  • •
    Fully rough regime: If ks+≥kRough+, the rough elements protrude into the fully turbulent region shifting the logarithmic profile downwards. In this flow regime, as shown in Fig. 10 (c), the viscous sublayer is entirely destroyed by the large turbulence mixing caused by roughness elements. The friction drag significantly increases due to pressure force on the roughness and is independent of the viscous effect (Reynolds number). The pressure loss becomes independent of the molecular viscosity of fluid and velocity when roughness elements intrude viscous sublayer [78].
kSmooth+and kRough+ are the onsets of transitionally rough and fully rough regimes, respectively. Different values for of kSmooth+andkRough+, reported in the literature, are listed in Table 2.

Table 2. Values for the lower and upper bands of transitionally rough regime.

ResearcherRoughness typekSmooth+kRough+
Nikuradse [287]Uniform sand-grain570
Ioselevich and Pilipenko [290]Sand-grain roughness2.590
Ligrani and Moffat [233]Packed sphere bed1550
Langelandsvik et al. [291]Commercial steel pipes1.418
Shockling et al. [292]Honed pipe3.530
Schultz and Flack [248]Surface scratch2.525
Lewkowicz and Musker [293]Ship-hull roughness (using hkrsm+)1740
Cebeci and Bradshaw [294]Sand-grain roughness2.2590
The variety of reported values for the onset of the transitionally rough and fully rough regimes for different roughness types obviously indicates the difficulty in definition of scaling parameters applicable for all roughness regimes. Clauser [292] claimed this difficulty on the fact that some roughness types generate roughness functions with monotonically changing slope while others possess inflection points.
The entire layer that dynamically influenced by the length scale associated with roughness elements is referred to as “roughness sublayer”. Fig. 10 (d) illustrates the schematic of velocity profile over roughness with the indication of roughness sublayer, logarithmic layer and outer layer. The roughness sublayer exists beneath the inertial or logarithmic layer and is the roughness counteract of the viscous sublayer. The roughness sublayer is extended to ≈ 2k − 5k, where k is the roughness height relative to the wall [21]. The utilisation of ks to define the extension of roughness sublayer instead of k is proposed by Schultz and Flack [237], since it provides a universal measure of the influence of the surface roughness on the mean flow. They showed that the roughness sublayer is extended to ≈ 3ks − 5ks.

4.3. “k-type” and “d-type” roughness

The terms k-type and d-type roughness are characteristics used for two-dimensional roughness such as spanwise ribs and grooves. The distinction between k-type and d-type roughness was initially suggested by Perry et al. [295], who observed that for some type of surface roughness the flow behaviour is similar to the usual Clauser or Nikuradse scheme; that is the rough-wall friction factor (f) - Reynolds number (Re) curve for constant Ue is identical to that of smooth walls for constant U (the same concept as that in the wall similarity hypothesis). They also stated that the resulting graph of U+versus kU*/ν is universal for a given roughness geometry and gives the relationship for both transitionally and fully rough flow regimes in terms of variables required for boundary layer analysis. However, Streeter & Chu [296] and Ambrose [297] have reported examples of different behaviour of flow over rough surfaces, whose friction factor-Reynolds number characteristics are sensitive to relative scale k/d. This type of roughness is characterised by a smooth surface with a series of depression or grooves which the outer flow generate stable vortices. In this case, as Perry et al. [295] showed, U+ is a function of the product Ref alone which is proportional to dU*/ν instead of kU*/ν. Since the characteristic length scale d was used for describing the roughness function, this result appears to be inconsistent with “law of the wall” for rough-wall flows developed by Nikuradse [287] and Clauser [298]. Based on these observations, Perry et al. [295] proposed two types of roughness, k-type and d-type, while the symbols denoting the significant length scale involved. They summarised previous evidence for d-type roughness behaviour and described the related mean velocity profile over d-type roughness. Basically, the d-type roughness is terminology for tightly packed ribs/grooves, while widely spaced ribs/grooves are of k-type roughness. The k-type two-dimensional roughness behaves similarly to the random three-dimensional roughness.
In a follow on from earlier works in this field, Coleman et al. [299] performed experiments of flow structures within the cavities between consecutive ribs of uniform cross-section. They outlined three distinctive types of roughness (Fig. 11) based on the pitch ratio L/H: the d-type, the intermediate type, and the k-type. Here L is the distance between ribs and H is the height of ribs.
Coleman et al. [299] observed that, for closely spaced d-type roughness, stable separated eddies occupy the entire cavity between ribs, with marginal disturbance of the outer flow. However, for widely spaced k-type roughness, reattachment occurs before the next rib, and eddies penetrating to the boundary-layer edge are shed from the roughness. A smooth transition from d-type flow to interactive k-type flow occurs at a rib spacing of W/h = 5. The structure of flow over ribs consist of two contraclockwise vortices and the mean flow profile is quasi-logarithmic above roughness tops, while the profile in the interfacial layer below roughness tops changing from exponential (for ribs of W/h < 10) to linear (W/h ≥ 10) to logarithmic (W/h ≫ 10) with increasing rib spacing.
More recently, Li and Li [300] performed experiments on turbulent open-channel flows over roughness elements. Below the crest, they observed weak eddies in the cavity between adjacent roughness elements for d-type (as illustrated in Fig. 11 (a)), while they indicated two eddies with different strength for the intermediate-type roughness (as illustrated in Fig. 11 (b)). They had evidence of boundary layer velocity structure for the k-type roughness with a small eddy on the windward side of a roughness element (as illustrated in Fig. 11 (c)). Some researchers have argued that the difference between k-type and d-type roughness relies on the state of the vortex shedding [301]. For k-type roughness, Perry et al. [295] suggested that eddies with a length scale of order k (roughness height) are injected into the flow above the crest of the roughness elements (vortex shedding) which diffuse to the flow further away from the roughness crests, while d-type roughness maintains stable eddies between roughness elements. However, Djenidi et al. [302] and Leonardi et al. [303] have reported vortex shedding into the flow for d-type roughness, although less intense compared to that of k-type roughness.
Jiménez [81] explained the behaviour of d-type roughness as being able to sustain stable recirculation vortexes that isolate the outer flow from the roughness, as illustrated in Fig. 11 (a). The d-type roughness can reduce the drag by trapping pockets of fluid between roughness elements [304] and is especially crucial to heat transfer applications [86]. Ghaddar et al. [305] numerically studied laminar flow over a grooved channel and found that the vortices bifurcate spontaneously to an oscillatory state at fairly low Reynolds numbers, and that the bifurcation eventually leads to subharmonic behaviour in which several grooves eject collectively. Ghaddar et al. [306] later studied DNS of enhanced heat transfer in channels by introducing pulsating flow at frequencies resonating with the natural instability, supporting the idea that similar resonances could occur naturally over d-type roughness. Walls with grooves wider than ≈ 3 − 4 k behave like k-type roughness (Fig. 11 (c)) sustaining recirculation vortexes ahead of ribs in the grooves [295,302,307].
Jiménez [81] employed the term roughness solidity (λ) to distinguish between k-type, and d-type roughness. The solidity is a parameter that quantifies the roughness density and is defined as the total projected frontal roughness area per unit wall-parallel projected area. Jiménez [81] outlined two flow regimes: the sparse regime and dense regime. In the sparse regime where the solidity is below λ ≈ 0.15, the impact of the roughness increases with solidity; however, in the dense one, it reduces since the roughness elements shelter each other. The sparse regime (λ < 0.15) and dense regime (λ > 0.15) have been reported by other researchers [250,268]. Jimenez [81] reported that flows over the k-type roughness could be characterised as sparse regimes while d-type roughness is in the dense regime category.
The Effective Slope, ES, is connected to the solidity parameter, λ, through the relation ES = 2λ [61,72,268]. MacDonald et al. [268] showed that the value of ES ≈ 0.35, defined as a demarcation point between waviness regime (ES < 0.35) and roughness regime (ES > 0.35), is associated with a solidity value of λ = 0.175, quite close to the value λ = 0.15 (defined by Jiménez [81]). Moreover, Mejia-Alvarez and Christensen [274]; De Marchis [308] have reported that ES = 0.35 is a limit between slope dependent and height dependent flows. They also reported that waviness regime can be attributed to the region where ES < 0.35 and viscous drag is dominant, while the transitionally rough region falls in the range 0.15 < ES < 0.35.
In the sparse regimes (k-type roughness), it is readily apparent that the extra drag imposed by roughness should be proportional to the frontal surface of the roughness elements and ks/k∼λ. Despite the utilisation of solidity for distinguishing between different roughness types, it cannot solely fully characterise a rough surface. For example, Jimenez [81] showed a dependency on λ−2, while powers down to λ−5 have been also proposed by Dvorak [309]. Other geometrical parameters are required to describe the mutual sheltering of the roughness elements. For d-type roughness, Perry et al. [295] observed that ks ≈ 0.02δ which shows that ks is independent of roughness dimensions. Similar results were reported by Jiménez [81], although he also observed inconsistency with a constant value for ks/δ. Bandyopadhyay [232] reported that turbulent rough-wall flows with δ/k < 40 behave less like d-type roughness; this is also the criterion where the wall similarity hypothesis is violated and roughness influences the outer layer.
Leonardi et al. [310] suggested that d-type behaviour is obtained when the origin of y is on the plane of the crests, and the frictional drag is much larger than the pressure drag. They asserted that the relative magnitude of the frictional and pressure drag could be used for the distinction between k-type and d-type roughness. However, a fully accurate distinction between roughness types has not been proposed so far. Most of the CFD models that account for surface roughness have been developed based on the observations of the turbulent flow structures over k-type roughness. There is conflicting evidence between turbulent flow over d-type and intermediate-type roughness and the available data from various studies does not point to an agreed conclusion [81]. Therefore, the d-type and intermediate-type roughness should be resolved by the computational grid to obtain accurate results compatible with the physics of fluid over this type of roughness.

5. Methods and correlations for the evaluation of ks

The equivalent sand-grain roughness ks, can be assigned to every type of roughness. For this reason, experiments must be performed to find the velocity distribution U(y) in the boundary layer close to the rough wall. Then, it can be written [311](21)ks=exp{κlimy→0[8.0+1κlny−U(y)τw/ρ]};where τw is the wall shear stress at y = 0. The flow condition must be checked to make sure that it is a fully rough regime. The value of ks proposed for a range of regular and technical rough surfaces can be found in Ref. [3,[312], [313], [314]]

5.1. Experimental studies

Most of the correlations of equivalent sand-grain roughness ks reported in the literature were based on the experimental data of turbulent flow in fully rough regimes. Several studies have suggested ks based on the Ra parameter. Among all, Foster [315] showed that ratios of ks/Ra  = 2 for typical machined-ground surfaces and ks/Ra  = 7 for emery papers with a range of grit size. Koch and Smith [316] found a value of ks/Ra  = 6 for emery paper while Bammert and Sandstede [317] estimated a value of ks/Ra  = 2 for typical milled surfaces.
However, Bogard [318] showed that using a single roughness parameter such as Ra is insufficient for characterising roughness effects. In a similar result, Goodhand et al. [319] reported that criteria defined only by the Ra parameter are oversimplified. Therefore, several researchers have defined the ks based on the other roughness features such as; moment of surface height probability density function (PDF) [82,277,320,321], roughness slope [283,322], and density of the roughness elements [280,281].
Musker [321] suggested the use of moments of PDF in the determination of the roughness scale. He then defined the sand-grain roughness height k, in terms of the Rq parameter but modified by the average roughness slope sp, skewness sk, and kurtosis ku as(22)k=Rq(1+asp)(1+bskku);where a and b are empirical constants to fit the data of naturally rough surfaces. Musker's correlation was developed based on five statistical parameters of rough surfaces and other attempts have been made by researchers to reduce the number of parameters. Townsin and Dey [323] applied another approach to define the sand-grain roughness height k, using the amplitude energy spectral density and a variable long wavelength cut-off to determine the roughness height based on the spectral area of painted ship roughness. Based on the results of 30 experimental sets of ship paint roughness, the best correlation for the roughness height was expressed as [323](23)k∼χm0m2=θm4m2;where θ is the spectral area, m2 and m4 are the slopes by the second and fourth moments respectively, while χ = θm4/m22 is the bandwidth parameter. Although this method proved promising in the fully rough regime, the correlation demonstrated poor agreement with the experimental data on the transitionally rough regime.
Determination of the roughness density requires a full 3D surface map which is hard to achieve for many practical surfaces such as turbine blades, while the surface roughness slope angle α is easier to obtain using 2D trace [283,322]. Bons [322] proposed a correlation for equivalent sand-grain roughness height based on the root-mean-square of local slope αrms. Subsequently, Bons [283] suggest using on the mean forward-facing roughness slope angle α¯f since it is easier to calculate in practice.
Based on the different methods of roughness characterisation, several correlations for the estimation of the equivalent sand-grain roughness have been proposed in the literature, and are listed in Table 3. The diverse variety of proposed equations in Table 3 demonstrates that a single correlation is not able to estimate the equivalent roughness height or all types of roughness. For example, Flack et al. [278] reported that correlations should be collated based on the positive, negative and zero skewness while Botros [324] suggested that ks can be calculated by fitting on Nikuradse or Colebrook roughness data using only Rq parameter. On the other hand, Dirling [281] and Sigal and Danberg [280] proposed a combined solidity and shape parameter, Λ, to predict ks while Bons [283,322] suggested the root-mean-square of local slope αrms.
