Flack et al. [278] demonstrated that correlations for waviness (ES < 0.35) and highly skewed surfaces must include more surface parameters including effective slope (for wavy surface), shape parameter, and length of the surface elevation. Recent studies have reported promising predictions of rough wall flows using the effective slope, ES, of roughness [61,64,72,249,308,327,328].
Irregular surface roughness is a natural consequence of Additive Manufacturing (AM) processes of metals which have recently received considerable attention among researchers. An example of surface roughness fabricated by AM is illustrated in Fig. 2 (g) in the introduction section. Stimpson et al. [59] studied the surface roughness of channels fabricated by AM. Their attempt to correlate the equivalent sand-grain roughness based on the approaches that existed in the literature (listed in Table 3) was unsuccessful. This was because of the significant difference between the roughness parameters of different test coupons and that the previous studies referred to were performed for external flows where walls did not constrain the boundary layer growth. Stimpson et al. [59] found that one of the simplest statistical measures of channel roughness (Ra/Dh) correlated best with ks/Dh and also reported that the modified roughness parameter suggested by van Rij et al. [325] is the most appropriate method for rough surfaces fabricated by the laser-based additive manufacturing method [325].

5.2. CFD studies

CFD has been used by several researchers for the evaluation of the proposed correlations in response to irregular and random roughness. The assessment of various correlations for irregular roughness is limited within the literature. Yuan and Piomelli [64] employed the Large Eddy Smulation (LES) method to evaluate the influence of different roughness correlation on the skin friction factor over four distinctive realistic roughness surfaces. They reported that correlations based on the roughness density [280,281] and roughness slope [283,322] can similarly predict the equivalent sand-grain roughness with better accuracy than moment-based correlations [82,277,320,321]. This is mainly because the spectral moments of the surface do not directly include the information on the slope [66]. This statement along with the aforementioned argument of Flack and Schultz [82] concerning the need for information on the roughness density, demonstrate that at least one parameter containing data on the effect of the roughness density or slope should be included in the methods for estimation of the flow characteristics over rough surfaces.
The equivalent sand-grain roughness height is a roughness scale in the fully rough regime, and is not suitable for the transitionally rough flow regime. The DNS method provides the ability to simulate realistic random roughness with a wide range of surface roughness parameters. Thakkar et al. [72] performed a DNS study for 17 irregular rough surfaces at the same friction Reynolds number (the Reynolds number obtained by applying the friction velocity). All surfaces are scaled to the same physical roughness height under the transitionally rough regime. They showed that the solidity (frontal area ratio), skewness, streamwise correlation length, and root mean square roughness height have a significant influence on the roughness function.
According to the above literature review, the equivalent sand-grain roughness appears to be correlated with distinctive sets of geometrical roughness parameters for different rough surfaces, and no universal correlation exists that can predict the flow over surfaces with irregular random roughness. Forooghi et al. [66] performed a DNS study of low Reynold flow over realistic regular roughness. They studied 38 distinctive roughness geometries considering a range of effective slope (0.2 < ES < 0.9), skewness ( − 0.33 < sk < 0.66), kurtosis (1.9 < ku < 2.7), and a new parameter Δ, accounting for the distribution of the roughness element size. They proposed a roughness correlation as(24a)ksRz={F~(sk)G~(ES)Δ≤0.15F(sk)G(ES)Δ>0.15where Rt is the maximum peak to valley height roughness height over several subsets of the surface. They defined different auxiliary functionsF~(sk),G~(ES), G(ES), and F(sk) to isolate the effect of each roughness parameters on the flow. These functions are expressed as(24b)F(sk)=0.67sk2+0.93sk+1.3(24c)F~(sk)={F(sk)Δ≥Δ0F(sk)[1+M(Δ−Δ0)]Δ<Δ0(24d)G(ES)=1.07[1−exp(−3.5ES)](24e)G~(ES)=1.05[1−exp(−3.8ES)]where Δ0 = 0.35 and M=1.47sk2−1.35sk−0.66.
More recently, Jouybari et al. [329] applied Deep Neural Network (DNN) and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) machine learning methods to develop a high-fidelity approach for prediction of the Nikuradse equivalent sand-grain roughness ks[329] for turbulent flows over a wide range or rough surfaces. They performed DNS study of 45 surfaces with different roughness topography which differ widely in moments of roughness height (Ra, sk, and ku), effective slope, average inclination, porosity, and degree of randomness. Among all surfaces employed in the DNS, 30 of them are identified as fully rough flow regimes. The combination of these 30 DNS results in combination with 15 fully rough experimental data sets of Flack et al. [277]; Barros et al. [330]; Flack et al. [330]; Flack et al. [278] are used for the calculation of ks using DNN and GPR. Using the correlation of ks proposed by Flack et al. [277] (see Table 3) as a baseline, the DNN and GPR methods predicted ks with an rms error of less than 10% and a maximum error of less than 30% which appears more accurate than the correlations existing in the literature. However, they did not suggest any correlation for calculation of ks.

6. Mean flow over rough walls

As mentioned earlier, current engineering models of the rough-wall turbulent models have been developed based on the extension to the smooth-wall turbulent flow models. This section describes the methods for the extension of the mean velocity and temperature profiles over smooth surfaces to that of rough surfaces. The major impact of the roughness is the perturbation of the turbulent boundary layer in such a way that leads to an increase in the wall shear stress, and ultimately, the augmentation of wall heat and mass transfer. This leads to the change of the velocity and temperature profiles near the wall. As shown in Fig. 10, depending on the rough flow regime, the viscous sublayer could partially (in transitionally rough regimes) or completely (in fully rough regimes) be destroyed by roughness. However, according to wall similarity hypothesis, the effect of the roughness on the flow is limited to the roughness sublayer, and the outer layer remains unaffected. In the roughness sublayer, the flow is highly disturbed due to the large turbulence mixing caused by roughness elements, so that three to five roughness heights above the surface is needed where the flow is outside the influence of the roughness elements [21,237,331]. Based on these observations, researchers have attempted to develop models for mean flow over surface roughness, based on the available models of smooth wall flows.
Fig. 12 compares the inner-layer mean velocity profile of smooth walls with different rough walls for zero pressure gradient turbulent boundary layer flow. For the rough surfaces, the similarity in the mean velocity profile is shown for all surfaces, while downward displacement (ΔU+) of the mean velocity profile below the smooth wall (velocity deficit) is observed. The similarity in the mean velocity profile in the overlap and outer layer indicates that the effect of the surface roughness is limited to the inner layer, which is in accordance with the wall similarity hypothesis.

6.1. Mean velocity profile over rough walls

Clauser [292,298] studied the effect of the surface roughness on the mean velocity distribution and presented a method that has demonstrated to be robust and widely applied. He argued that the velocity profile in the viscous sublayer for rough surfaces follows a logarithmic pattern with a similar slope as for smooth surfaces, as illustrated in Fig. 12. He also found that the sole impact of the roughness is a downward shift of the log-law profile as a function of the roughness Reynolds number, as illustrated in Fig. 12. Clauser [298] and Hama [332] each in an independent study introduced a parameter called roughness function (ΔU+) to emulate the effect of the velocity shift caused by surface roughness. They observed that the surface roughness shifts the logarithmic profile downwards, commensurate with ΔU+, indicating a shortage in the momentum compared to smooth walls. The velocity shift is proportional to lnks+ [333] and is independent of wall distance [334]. The shift velocity and roughness function is also a result of wall similarity for characterizing the roughness effect on the mean flow. These have been experimentally validated with numerous experiments including the works of Karen A. Flack and Michael P. Schultz and their colleagues [82,223,[235], [236], [237],[241], [242], [243], [244], [245], [246], [247], [248], [249], [250], [251]] and also Kenneth T. Christensen and his colleagues [87,224,225,[252], [253], [254], [255], [256], [257]] as well as recent DNS studies [[71], [72], [73],[258], [259], [260]].
The equilibrium boundary layer flow over rough walls comprises two overlapping regions; an outer layer scaling with u* and δ, and an inner layer scaling with ν/u* and all length scales required to thoroughly characterise roughness (e.g. roughness height, kurtosis, skewness, etc.). It is evident that the velocity profile also depends on the distance from the wall y itself. However, the definition of the origin of y for rough walls requires careful attention, since the roughness itself dislocates the entire flow in y-direction normal to the wall. To account for this, the displaced height is defined as Y = y − d, where d is the “fluid dynamic height origin” or “zero-plane displacement” depending on both flow and roughness characteristics.
Clauser [298] proposed the logarithmic velocity distribution for turbulent flow over rough walls as(25)U+=1κlny++C−ΔU+;where C is the smooth-wall intercept and κ is the von Kármán constant. He also asserted that the roughness function ΔU+ is a sole function of roughness Reynolds number ks+.
Hama [332] performed an extensive experimental study and proposed the roughness function for fully rough flows as(26)ΔU+=1κlnks++C−B;
Schlichting [76] proved that B is a constant value of 8.5 for fully rough flow regime in pipes. A similar value was reported by Pimenta et al. [335] for fully rough boundary layer over uniform sphere roughness. The relationship proposed for velocity profile by Clauser [298] and the roughness function by Hama [332] are both universal for given roughness geometry in pipes, channels, and zero pressure gradient boundary layer flows. Perry & Joubert [336] demonstrated that this universality extends to boundary layer flows in adverse pressure gradients.
The relationship proposed by Clauser [298] and Hama [332] are confined to the inner layer. By using Coles’ “law-of-the-wake” [90], the correlation can be extended to cover both the overlap and outer region of the boundary layer as [90](27)U+=1κlny++C−ΔU++Π(x)κw(yδ);
Flack and Schultz [250] in a review of their 15 years of experimental research of turbulent flow on rough surfaces stated that since no “universal” roughness function exists, no single roughness length scale can characterize all roughness types in all roughness regimes. They also showed that in the fully rough regime, the hydraulic roughness length scale is related to the root-mean-square roughness height and skewness; however, the onset of roughness effects could be associated with the largest surface features which are characterised by the peak-to-valley height. Moreover, the behaviour of roughness function in the transitionally rough regime is complicated and varies significantly between roughness types.
ABL flow over rough terrains such as plant and urban canopies is classified as fully rough since the roughness elements (obstacles) are so large that the laminar sublayer is completely destroyed and the flow is considered to be independent of the molecular viscosity [337]. In ABL flow analysis, the roughness sublayer is generally represented by an aerodynamic roughness length scale y0, which matches the smooth wall log-law profile, thus the velocity profile for rough walls reads as [21,338](28)U+=1κln(y−dy0);where d is zero-plane displacement which is required to fix the origin of y. Basically, d is a fluid dynamic property that represents the mean level of momentum absorption by the rough surface [21]. More discussion on calculation of zero-plane displacement d can be found elsewhere [21,233,295,339]. Eq. (28) is only valid in the fully rough regime; therefore, the hydraulic (or aerodynamic) roughness length y0 is an alternative scale that is similar to the equivalent sand-grain roughness height ks, imposing collapse to a single profile in the fully rough regime and can be set to y0 = ks/32.6 as suggested by Schlichting [3].

6.2. Roughness functions

The roughness function (ΔU+) emulates the effect of the velocity shift caused by surface roughness as a downward shift to the log-law profile. Roughness functions suggested in the literature have been correlated based on the collapse to either traditional Nikuradse [287,288] data with three distinctive functions for each roughness regimes (referred as to “Nikuradse-type” roughness function) or Colebrook et al. [340] data with single expression function (referred as to “Colebrook-type” roughness function).
In the hydraulically smooth regime, the perturbations caused by roughness elements are completely damped out by molecular viscosity, resulting in that ΔU+ = 0. In the transitionally rough regime, with increasing ks+ the roughness elements start to produce drag force, which influences the surface frictional drag and augments the roughness function. In the fully rough regime, the drag on the surface is entirely due to pressure drag on the roughness elements. The limit between these flow regimes depends on the roughness type [341]. The general form of Nikuradse-type roughness function can be written as [342](29)ΔU+={0ks+≤kSmooth+1κln[Csks+]×sin(π2lnks+−lnkS+lnkR+−lnkS+)kSmooth+<ks+≤kRough+1κln[Csks+]ks+>kRough+where Cs is the roughness constant and depends on the type of roughness. Nikuradse's resistance data for pipes roughened with tightly packed, uniform sand-grain roughness suggests the value of 0.5 for the roughness constant. If the type of roughness departs from the uniform sand-grain, other values should be adapted. Experimental evidence for non-uniform sand-grains, ribs, and wire-mesh roughness, recommends a higher value (Cs = 0.5 − 10). Cebeci and Bradshaw [294] recommended: kSmooth+=2.25, kRough+=90 and Cs = 0.253 for traditional Nikuradse roughness function and Cs = 0.5 for other type of roughness. The values of kSmooth+=3, kRough+=15 and Cs = 0.26 were proposed by Demirel et al. [343] with fitting the roughness function proposed by Schultz and Flack [248].
White [344] suggested a Colebrook-type roughness function, given by(30)ΔU+=1κln(1+0.3ks+)
Grigson [340] proposed an alternative Colebrook-type roughness function for the entire roughness Reynolds number based on the data of Colebrook and White [289] and Colebrook et al. [340], written as(31)ΔU+=1κln{1+ks+exp[κ(8.5−C)]}where κ = 0.41 and C = 5.25.
Reviews on roughness functions can be found in Bradshaw [345] and Flack and Schultz [82] and more recently by Andersson et al. [342].
In dense roughness regime, the roughness function does not scale with ks+; therefore, an additional factor requires to be taken into account for scaling turbulent flows for all roughness regimes. Fig. 13 illustrates the variation of roughness function ΔU+ with effective slope (ES) for different type of roughness available in the literature. It is clear that, for sparse roughness regime (ES > 0.35), ΔU+ does not scale with ES; however, in the dense roughness regime, ΔU+ decreases with increasing ES, which is consistent with the observation in d-type roughness. The reason for this observation can be attributed to a reduction in the Reynolds shear stress in near wall region that is being pushed away from the rough wall by near wall turbulent cycles [346]. Fig. 13 also shows that, for similar roughness type, ΔU+ for the surface with positive skewness (peak-dominated surface) are larger than that with a negative skewness (valley dominated surface).
More recently, De Marchis et al. [328] proposed a universal roughness function by performing large eddy simulation (LES) study as well as using other independent data in Refs [61,72,308,347].(32)ΔU+=1κln(ES.k*)+B*where k* is roughness Reynolds number either based on the mean roughness height, k+¯, or based on the root mean square of the roughness krms+. B* is a constant to fit the data which is equal to 3.5 for the correlation between ΔU+ and ES.krms+, while it becomes 4 for the correlation between ΔU+ and ES.k+¯.

6.3. Mean temperature profile

The Reynolds analogy can be used for the estimation of temperature profile over smooth surfaces. However, the Reynold analogy is not maintained for rough surfaces [349], [350], [351] since the physics of rough-wall momentum, and heat transfer boundary layers are not similar [352,353].
Several studies have been performed to obtain the mean temperature profile over rough surfaces. Kays and Crawford [78] suggested an alternative simplified formulation for the thermal law of the wall, which has been used for decades. Kays and Crawford's temperature profile reads as(33)T+=ΔT0++Prtκln(32.6y+ks+);Where Prt is the turbulent Prandtl number. The Reynolds analogy assumption can be replicated by settingΔT0+=0, indicating the elimination of the conduction sublayer for the fully rough regime. In fully rough regime, the viscous sublayer in the momentum boundary layer is completely destroyed and vanished while the conduction sublayer still exists in the thermal boundary layer. Therefore, heat transfer over rough surfaces is limited by conduction heat transfer in all rough flow regimes. The ΔT0+ is determined empirically and accounts for the conductive heat transfer in semi-stagnant fluid in roughness cavities [78]. Several empirical models for ΔT0+ have been proposed in the literature. Dipprey and Sabersky [352] and Owen and Thomson [353] suggested an empirical correlation for the thermal correction ΔT0+as(34)ΔT0+=1Cthks+mPrn;where Cth, m, and n are empirical constants. Dipprey and Sabersky [352] assigned the values of m = 0.2 and n = 0.44. A commonly used value of Cthis 0.8 based on the experiments over closely packed spherical roughness elements. Owen and Thomson [353] determined m = 0.45 and n = 0.8 for 3D flow across cavities and the value of Cth is assigned to 1.92 for randomly shaped roughness. However, Kays and Crawford [78] suggested Cth = 0.8, m = 0.2, and n = 0.44 based on the Pimenta et al. [335] experimental study on the closely packed spherical roughness elements. In most ice accretion studies [354], [355], [356], the coefficients proposed by Owen and Thomson [353] have been used. Goldberg and Batten [357] suggested Cth = 0.67, m = 0.15, and n = 0.8 while they reported that these constants may need small corrections depending on the roughness shape.
The influence of the surface roughness on the pressure drop is more than that heat transfer increase since the heat transfer enhancement is mainly due to the increase in the surfaces heat transfer area caused by roughness [352]. This issue becomes prominent for large roughness elements [358] where Kays and Crawford model fails to completely model the effect of the roughness. Therefore, some researchers have used a surface shape parameter Scorr [331,358,359] to account for the increased heat transfer area by rough surfaces compared to that of smooth surfaces. Alternatives to the correlations of Kays and Crawford [78] have been proposed by Ligrani and Moffat [233], Radenac et al. [358], Sucec [360] and Aupoix [359].

7. Roughness effects on fluid flow and heat transfer

As discussed earlier in the paper, roughness can influence heat and momentum transfer in the boundary layer. This influence can be observed through increasing pressure drop, altering flow laminar-turbulent transitions, inducing secondary flow motions, improving flow mixing, and enhancing heat transfer. This section briefly discusses three main roughness effects, comprising roughness induced pressure drop, roughness induced laminar-turbulent transition, and roughness induced secondary flow motions.
Generally, rough surfaces can be classified into two categories [361,362]: 2D roughness and 3D roughness. The term 2D roughness refers to surfaces with a linear profile such as spanwise or stream-wise ribs and groves with different cross-sections which are favourable for heat transfer applications [363], [364], [365], [366], [367], [368]. The term 3D roughness refers to surfaces with areal height maps that consist of regular or irregular roughness elements that are systematically/randomly distributed on a surface. A large number of studies have measured the statistical parameters of a wide range of regular and irregular surface roughness fabricated by additive manufacturing [57], [58], [59], roughness generated on the turbine blades [369], and other types of roughness [250,277,341,[370], [371], [372]].

7.1. Roughness induced pressure drop

The form drag and blockage effect induced by roughness elements lead to pressure drop in pipe and channel flows. Early studies focused mainly on the influence of the surface roughness on the pressure drop in pipes and friction losses in boundary layer flows, especially for turbulent flows. Darcy [2] conducted an experimental study of pipe flows with varying roughness, and later, Fanning [373] suggested a correlation for pressure drop in water pipes, including the effect of the wall roughness. These pioneering studies have initiated the field of rough-wall turbulent flows that led to a great deal of theoretical, experimental, and numerical studies in this field.
Nikuradse [287,288] coated the inner wall of pipes with uniformly sized sand grains and investigated the effect of wall roughness on the pressure drop for a range of Reynolds numbers and pipe diameters. Nikuradse found that, although surface roughness has a negligible impact on laminar flows, it considerably influences turbulent flows. He also demonstrated that the rougher the surface, the greater the friction, and therefore a greater pressure loss. On the other hand, for flows with specific combinations of relative roughness and Reynolds number categorised as hydrodynamically smooth regimes, the roughness does not affect the flow friction factor. In hydrodynamically smooth regimes, the average height of the surface roughness elements is much less than the thickness of the viscous sublayer; thus the roughness is not able to influence the turbulent flow over the viscous sublayer. Later, Colebrook [340] conducted experimental studies on the effect of roughness on the flow friction factor in pipes of various diameters, with various linings and roughness ranges. He correlated the results in the well-known Colebrook equation as follows:(35)1fDarcy0.5=−2.0log(ks/Dt3.7+2.51RefDarcy0.5)
Moody [374] employed the Colebrook equation and plotted the Darcy friction factor “fDarcy“ as a function of Reynolds number (Re) for the ratio of equivalent sand-grain roughness height to the tube diameter (ks/Dt) range of 0 to 0.05, resulting in the well-known Moody diagram that can be used for all flow regimes.
In the transitionally rough regime, the Moody diagram can considerably overestimate the pressure drop as reported by Allen et al. [375] and Langelandsvik et al. [291] for honed steel pipes and commercial steel pipes respectively. This implies that the Colebrook correlation employed in the formulation of the Moody diagram may not apply to a wide range of roughness of engineering interest. Fortunately, from an engineering point of view, this overestimation is on the conservative side. Other shortcomings of the Moody diagram include the lack of an appropriate definition of roughness length scale and the limited applicability of the prescribed surfaces and their roughness properties to many other materials and surfaces. Improved versions of the Moody diagram have been proposed, and LaViolette [376], in a review of the Moody diagram and its alternatives in the literature, proposed a novel alternative to Moody diagram shown to generate a solution without iteration for any type of pipe flow.
The Colebrook equation cannot be rearranged to calculate the friction factor due to the implicit representation of the friction factor “ fDarcy” in the formula. Therefore, it can be solved only iteratively or by employing explicit approximation which introduces certain errors associated with calculations. Other empirical relations have been developed that provided good predictions of friction factor without an iterative process. For example, Gregory and McEnery [377] suggested a non-iterative correlation for prediction of friction factor that matches Colebrook's data. Brkic´ and Ojbašic [378] applied the genetic algorithm to optimise explicit approximations of Colebrook's equation to improve the accuracy of prediction. Flack and Schultz [82] proposed a new correlation for the calculation of the overall friction drag coefficient Cf in rough pipes using data on a wide range of surface roughness and roughness elements comprising commercial pipe [291], honed (scratch) [248], sand-grain [247], gravel [231], honed pipe [326], pyramids [249], and packed spheres with grit [237].
The reduction of channel/pipe cross-section area (which is also referred to as channel/pipe size) can increase the effect of the surface roughness on the fluid flow and heat transfer [379], [380], [381], [382], [383], [384], [385], [386], specifically in mini-channels (channels with a hydraulic diameter (Dh) between 200 µm to 3 mm) and microchannels (channels with a Dh between 10 µm to 200 µm). Dai et al. [379] reviewed 33 articles, including 5569 experimental data points on liquid flow in rough micro- and mini-channels. They reported no apparent effect on the friction factor and the critical Reynolds number for relative roughness (the ratio of roughness hight to the channel hydraulic diameter) lower than 1%. They also found that the geometry of the cross-section (circular, triangular, rectangular) of channels have a marginal impact on the friction factor. Recent studies have shown that roughness can influence laminar flows in pipe and channels [387], [388], [389], by increased head loss due to increased dissipation rate [389] and the modification of the development region in internal flows [387]. Ghajar and his colleagues [390], [391], [392], [393], [394], [395], [396], [397] showed that increasing the surface roughness contributes to increased friction factor in laminar flow regimes in both micro- and mini-tubes.
Taylor et al. [398] reviewed the historical understanding, current perspective, and possible future development of the effects of surface roughness and texture on fluid flow and reported the limitation of the Moody diagram for relative surface roughness greater than 5%. A new modified diagram was presented for relative roughness up to 14%, which included the constricted flow effects of micro-and mini-channels. Therefore, classical theories of heat transfer and pressure drop for large-size channels has to be revised for channels with hydraulic diameters smaller than 1 mm [382,[399], [400], [401]]. Kandlikar et al. [402] showed that, apart from an increase in shear stress, surface roughness imposes flow area restrictions in microchannels that can further influence the pressure drop. To take these effects into account, they redefined Reynolds number and friction factors based on the “constricted flow diameter”, Dcf, as.(36)Dcf=Dt−2k,where Dcf is the constricted flow diameter, Dt is the tube diameter, and k is the roughness height. The friction factor based on the constricted diameter is related to the friction factor based on the tube diameter as follow(37)fDarcy,cf=fDarcy(Dt−2kDt).
In laminar flows, the Darcy friction factor for circular tubes is expressed based on the Reynolds number calculated using Dcf as(38)fDarcy,cf=64Recf.
In turbulent flows, the Colebrook equation is redefined based on the constricted flow diameter as(39)1(DtDt−2ε)2.5fDarcy,cf0.5=−2.0log(ε/Dt3.7+2.51Recf(DtDt−2ε)3.5fDarcy0.5)
In summary, the Moody diagram and Colebrook correlation overestimate the friction factor [291,375], and for more accurate predictions, relations proposed by Brkic´ and Ojbašic [378] and Flack and Schultz [82] can be used. The Moody diagram and Colebrook correlation can be applied to predict friction factor in tubes and channels with small relative roughness, less than 5% [398] and for microchannels, the modified correlation of Kandlikar et al. [402] can be employed.

7.2. Roughness induced laminar-turbulent transition

Many research studies have been devoted to how roughness can influence the laminar-turbulent transition point, which is of significant practical importance. In turbomachines, most of the blades quickly become rough as a result of deposition as well as mechanical or chemical damage. Surface roughness can modify the flow characteristics by introducing flow instabilities which can have a significant influence on the laminar-turbulent transition location [403,404].
In an attached boundary layer under very low-level flow disturbance (free stream turbulence intensity less than 0.5%) natural laminar-turbulent transition occurs [405]. This process is initiated by the generation of exponentially growing 2D waves known as Tollmien-Schlichting (TS) waves (primary instability). This is followed by a 3D instability (secondary instability) leading to significant 3D flows with the formation of streamwise/spanwise vortices. The final stage of such a transition process is the breakdown stage. The large scale vortices break down into smaller structures, generating turbulent spots that eventually merge to form a turbulent boundary layer [76,406].
In the presence of certain sources of sufficiently high flow disturbance, for example, freestream turbulence larger than 1% [407] or surface roughness [408], the laminar-turbulent transition occurs more rapidly, and 2D instability stage of natural transition is bypassed. This type of laminar-turbulent transition is referred to as “bypass transition”. Bypass transition comprises three main regions [407]: the buffeted laminar boundary layer, the region of intermittent turbulent spot formation, and the fully turbulent boundary layer. In the buffeted laminar boundary layer, the shear amplification leads to elongated streaks in the streamwise velocity fluctuations, as shown in Fig. 14. In the intermediate region, the localised perturbations initiate instabilities that eventually evolve into turbulent spots. Once the turbulent spots fully formed, they propagate laterally and grow longitudinally until overtake the main turbulent region. Bypass transition was extensively studied by Paul Durbin and his colleagues [407,[409], [410], [411], [412], [413], [414], [415], [416], [417], [418], [419], [420], [421], [422], [423]]. They investigated mechanisms involved in this type of laminar-turbulent transition and developed related numerical models.
In general, surface roughness moves the onset of laminar-turbulent transition upstream within the flow by bypassing the primary instability. Smaller levels of roughness destabilize the mean flow through a linear amplification of the primary instabilities [425] while larger ones bypass primary instabilities by distorting the flow locally [408,425,426]. Extensive experimental and CFD studies have been performed on the flow laminar-turbulent transition over different roughness, including isolated roughness as well as 2D, and 3D roughness elements distributed on the surface. Durbin [413] reported that, although a significant body of studies has revealed the aspects of laminar-turbulent transition mechanisms due to isolated roughness [276,[427], [428], [429]], bypass transition caused by distributed roughness has not been fully understood. It is found that the low-speed flow behind an isolated element of roughness lifts up from the wall creating an unstable wake or horseshoe vortices. Then, a laminar-turbulent transition is followed by the algebraic amplification of the individual disturbance evolving into streak-like motions. In addition to this, an unstable detached shear layer over the isolated roughness element further accelerate the transition process.
The mechanism of laminar-turbulent transition over distributed roughness is probably related to the formation of streaks by roughness in a similar manner as free stream turbulence flow does. This means that bypass transition may be triggered due to the flow disturbance from the perturbations caused by surface roughness at the wall instead of free-stream turbulence [430]. Fig. 15 illustrates the laminar-turbulent boundary layer transition over a surface covered with 3D distributed roughness, adopted from Vadlamani et al. [409]. It shows that the streamwise streaks are steady earlier and subsequently become unsteady and secondary instabilities develop over the streaks. At this point, hairpin vortices begin to generate, leading to the development of the downstream sustained turbulent flow.
Recent studies have observed the development of a shear layer on the distributed roughness elements. For example, Muppidi and Mahesh [431] reported counter-rotating pairs of streamwise vortices developed underneath the shear layer. The interaction of theses counteracting vortices along with the shear layer contribute to laminar-turbulent transition. Vadlamani et al. [409] performed DNS of laminar-turbulent transition over distributed roughness considering the effect of the roughness height. They demonstrated that transient mechanisms alter substantially with the increasing roughness height. For roughness elements that are positioned inside the boundary layer, the elevated shear layer induced by roughness elements changes high- and low-speed streaks near the wall, destabilising the shear layer and promoting a transition to turbulence. For roughness elements larger than the boundary layer thickness, turbulent wakes created behind the roughness elements promote a transition to turbulence. The distributed roughness causes the laminar-turbulent transition point to advance and increases skin friction or turbulent heating [403]. Due to the transition from laminar to turbulence, the heat transfer coefficient can increase by a factor of 10 [432]. Detailed information on the effect of different distributed roughness on the laminar-turbulent transition can be found elsewhere [319,404,[433], [434], [435]].
Fig. 16 indicates an image of temperature distribution over an aerofoil, recorded by Goodhand et al. [319], which is half rough (sandblasted) and half smooth. The lighter region indicates the turbulent flow, while the darker area identifies the laminar flow. As shown in Fig. 16, it is clear that the roughness causes the location of laminar-turbulent transition to jump to the leading edge in discrete locations referred to as turbulent wedges [319].
Boyle and Stripf [320] showed that, for a fixed roughness height, the transition to turbulence moves forward with increasing Reynolds number demonstrating a reduction in the aerodynamic efficiency of turbine blade cascade. Conversely, at low Reynolds numbers, Boyle and Senyitko [436] reported that, at low Reynolds numbers, surface roughness improves the aerodynamic efficiency of gas turbines by reducing losses at low turbulence intensity; however, at high Reynolds numbers, roughness approximately doubles the vane pressure drop. In a review by Bons [5], a specific region of “roughness benefit” at low Reynolds numbers was reported. This suggests the importance of exploring the influence of the roughness on the fluid flow for enhanced efficiency (both thermal and aerodynamic). More information on roughness induced laminar-turbulent transition can be found elsewhere [429,437].
Surface roughness can also influence the laminar-turbulent transition in microchannels, which is frequently referred to as roughness induced laminar-turbulent transition. Kandlikar and colleagues in various studies [384,385,402,[438], [439], [440], [441], [442], [443], [444], [445], [446], [447], [448], [449]] on microchannels, demonstrated that for high relative roughness, the laminar-turbulent transition occurred at lower Reynolds numbers (as low as 350) and the friction factor was approximately three times larger than predicted by conventional theory. In systematic studies on micro- and mini-tubes with circular cross-sections, Ghajar and his colleagues [390], [391], [392], [393], [394], [395], [396], [397] showed that increasing the surface roughness caused the earlier onset and end of laminar-turbulent transition.
As reported by Schlichting and Gersten ([311] pp. 472 and 473), further effects of the roughness on laminar-turbulent transition could be reflected as flexible wall (inducing elastic wave in the wall), boundary layer oscillations that influence the outer flow, and wave-shaped temperature variations.

7.3. Roughness induced secondary flow

Secondary flows are the occurrence of noticeable fluid motions perpendicular to the main flow direction in wall-bounded flows. Secondary motions of turbulent flow in non-circular cross-section ducts were first observed by Nikuradse [450] with different types of secondary motions then introduced and categorised by Prandtl [451] into two types: first kind, and second kind secondary flows. Prandtl's first kind secondary flow occurs in curved channels/pipes of any cross-section geometry due to centrifugal force which prevails in both turbulent and laminar flows. Prandtl's second kind secondary flow takes place in turbulent flow in non-circular cross-section ducts and is related to inhomogeneities of the Reynolds stresses [452]. It can also occur in plane or symmetrical wall-bounded flows if a local spanwise heterogeneity in wall conditions exists, for example, due to surface roughness.
Despite its weak intensity, secondary motion can significantly influence the flow and alter the mean velocity profile due to the generation of local streamwise vorticity. The spanwise inhomogeneity introduces distinct gradients into the Reynolds stress distribution and alters local flow turbulent properties. These gradients lead to an imbalance of local turbulent production and dissipation rate, which in order to fulfil the balance, inherently translates into the generation of local streamwise vorticity [453,454]. This eventually leads to the formation of large-scale vortex pairs occupying the entire boundary layer thickness, as shown in Fig. 17, and can significantly alter the mean velocity profile. While these large-scale features are strongly evident in the averaged velocity field, the corresponding instantaneous secondary flow fields do not directly reveal their existence [455]. The application of secondary flow for heat transfer enhancement has been studied by researchers; including improved heat transfer by the generation of the secondary flow of Prandtl's first kind in curved tubes [456], [457], [458] and Prandtl's second kind by roughness [368,[459], [460], [461]].
The formation of secondary motions over surfaces roughened with flow-aligned roughness strips in ducts was demonstrated in the pioneering work of Hinze [453]. Later, Hinze [454] hypothesised that the formation of secondary flows is a consequence of the production–dissipation imbalance of turbulent kinetic energy over spanwise heterogeneity. The effect of the secondary flow induced by spanwise inhomogeneity was reported as the thickening and thinning of boundary layer thickness in the cross-plane of the boundary layer [462], [463], [464], [465], [466], as shown in Fig. 17. This is due to the formation of low momentum pathways (LMP) associated with upwelling motion and high momentum pathways (HMP) associated with downwelling motions above the surfaces [463,467,468].
In spite of diverse configurations of spanwise inhomogeneity, two main configurations have been well studied in recent decades [69,469,470]: ridge-type roughness and strip-type roughness. Ridge-type roughness consists of spanwise variations of local elevation of the wall, as shown in Fig. 17 (a), while strip-type roughness comprises of spanwise variations in wall-shear stress, as shown in Fig. 17 (b). For ridge-type roughness, the upwelling and downwelling movements were indicated above the elevated and recessed wall areas, respectively [455,464,[471], [472], [473]]. Therefore, secondary flows occur somewhere near the junction between the raised and recessed sections of the surface, with the upwelling either above the junction [470] or above the ridge [466,474,475], as shown in Fig. 17 (a). On the other hand, Strip-type roughness generates upwelling motion over the smooth wall (the low-shear region) and a downwelling motion over the rough walls (the high-shear region) [467,470,476]. Therefore, the secondary flow is placed above the interface between the roughness and smooth surface, as shown in Fig. 17 (b).
Previous studies on ridge-type roughness have investigated flat surfaces with the elevated parts comprising of many possible cross-sectional shapes: rectangular [466,472,477,478], triangular [471,478,479], semicircle [478], trapezoidal [474], streamwise-aligned pyramids [480], and smoother, sinusoidal-like spanwise elevation variations [470,475,481]. Combinations of both ridge-type and strip-type roughness also have been studied in the literature [69,455,464]. Fig. 18 illustrates a schematic of an open channel with combinations of both ridge-type and strip-type roughness at the channel's wall used in a DNS study of secondary flow motions by Stroh et al. [69]. Fig. 18 (a) shows the configuration of the open channels, while Fig. 18 (b) indicates three considered elevations of strip-type roughness relative to the smooth surface (channel wall): h = 0, k¯, and 2k¯. Stroh et al. [69] observed the formation of counteracting rotations for the same type of the roughness topography, as shown in Fig. 19, depending on whether it is introduced as protruding roughness (h = 0) or recessed roughness (h=2k¯). Fig. 19 demonstrates that changing the elevation of the strip-type roughness is an additional parameter for influencing the arrangement the secondary flow motion from ridge-type (h = 0) regime to strip-type regime (h=2k¯). In the intermediate state (Fig. 19 (b)), a more elaborate secondary flow topology is created. In this case, the counteracting vortex pair in the lower channel half are associated with the one observed for h=2k¯ and the small ones positioned in the centre of the roughness with h = 0.
Other studies with different spanwise heterogeneity have been studied in the literature; including surfaces with multiple spanwise roughness wavelengths [463], alternating arrangements of directional/anisotropic rough surfaces [465], and converging-diverging riblets [462,465,482]. Converging–diverging riblets also produce secondary flows even in laminar flows [483], where no spanwise gradients in Reynolds shear stress occur and suggest a different generation mechanism to secondary flows of Prandtl's second kind. Experimental observations of the formation of secondary flow over turbine blades with irregular roughness have also been reported (see, e.g. Mejia-Alvarez & Christensen [274]and Barros & Christensen [463]).
In the numerical simulation, strip roughness can be modelled as spanwise alternating regions of high and low wall shear stress (τR and τs in Fig. 17) implemented directly as boundary conditions (e.g. Willingham et al. [467]; Chung et al. [476]). A similar method can be used for superhydrophobic surfaces, with spanwise-alternating no-slip and free-slip boundary conditions (e.g. Jelly et al. [484]; Türk et al. [485]; Lee et al. [486]; Stroh et al. [487]).
In practice, the formation of spanwise roughness inhomogeneity exactly aligned with the flow is unlikely. However, this phenomenon can particularly be related to spatially non-uniform roughness formation over turbomachinery blades reported by Bons et al. [369]. The formation of secondary flow motion over damaged turbine blades has been observed by Mejia-Alvarez and Christensen [274] and Barros & Christensen [463]. Strif et al. [459,488] reported induced secondary flow by roughness dominate the heat transfer distribution on the turbine vanes. The spanwise heterogeneous ridge type roughness has been extensively used for drag reduction and heat transfer augmentation, as reviewed by Soleimani and Eckels [30]. They stated that ridge type roughness lifts the large-scale turbulent vortices from the near-wall region and controls the turbulent coherent structures leading to reduced shear stress. The secondary flow motion induced by ridge type roughness enhances flow mixing and increases heat transfer. In river flows, large-scale bed elements elongated parallel with the primary flow is characterized by ridge-type and/or strip-type roughness [470,489,490]. Such bed forms induce secondary flows and trigger lateral sediment transport, boosting and maintaining longitudinal bedforms [491], [492], [493].

7.4. The effect of streamwise roughness inhomogeneity

The inhomogeneity in roughness distribution can occur in spanwise direction (as discussed in the previous section), streamwise direction [494,495], or combination of these surface changes [496], [497], [498]. Streamwise roughness heterogeneity prevails in numerous engineering wall-bounded turbulent flows. For example, the roughness condition changes occur at the interface between forest and grassland or the bio-fouled patches on the hull of a ship. Such streamwise heterogeneities can take place in a wide range of configuration, among which rough-to-smooth (RTS) and smooth-to-rough (STR), as shown in Fig. 20, are mostly studied in the literature.
The surface change triggers various phenomena that lead to the deviation of the near-wall flow from the equilibrium state. The near-wall flow accelerates due to the RTS surface changes [495,499], while it decelerates due to STR surface changes [494,500]. The near-wall flow influenced by the new surface is known as Internal Boundary Layer (IBL) [501], [502], [503] and is characterised by a thickness of δi(x). The flow away from the wall remains unaffected by surface change and still carries the history from the upstream surface (Fig. 20). The lower part of the IBL that has reached equilibrium with the new surface is referred to as Internal Equilibrium Layer (IEL) and is characterised by a thickness of δe(x). The influence of the new surface condition starts from the beginning of the surface change and gradually propagates towards the interior of the flow with transitioning downstream of the flow.
In the literature, flow recovery after streamwise-varying roughness has been studied theoretically [504], [505], [506], [507], numerically, and experimentally. Wind tunnel experiments have been conducted for flow over a fabricated RTS and STR surface change with roughness geometries composed of square bars [494,495,500,508], mesh roughness [509], [510], [511], transversely grooved surface [512], or grit roughness [511]. Krampa-Morlu and Balachandar [513] performed an experimental study of RTS flow recovery with d-type and intermediate-type rib roughness. They showed that the intermediate-type roughness had a higher roughness effect. Cheng and Castro [514] conducted an experimental study of flow field downstream of a step change, where the roughness height becomes ten-fold of the downstream roughness.
In the literature, related computational studies have been performed using roughness modelling such as wall-modelled LES, RANS as well as direct resolving of roughness with DNS. The widely used wall model for LES is the equilibrium logarithmic-law of the wall [163,515], and its extension to non-neutral flow using M-O similarity [516,517]. Saito and Durbin [518] developed a wall-modelled LES to investigate the turbulent flow transition over a smooth-rough-smooth step change. They reported an overshoot and undershoot immediately after the step change, which has been predicted before by other researchers [504,505,[519], [520], [521]]. A few studies have conducted direct resolving of roughness using DNS of flow with different roughness configurations, including 3D sinusoidal surface [522], rib roughness [523], [524], [525], and cube roughness [430,526].
Flow recovery over streamwise-varying roughness involves various flow phenomena, two of which are widely addressed in the literature: (i) the departure from equilibrium, and (ii) the formation of an internal boundary layer (IBL).

7.4.1. Departure from equilibrium

Generally, the majority of the flow within IBL is still non-equilibrium with the local wall condition, and a small portion of δi is taken up by δe (approximately 5 %) [527,528]. Most of the experimental and numerical studies have evaluated the flow characteristics from a certain y+, assumed as departure from equilibrium. Among all, Carper and Porte-Agel [509] conducted an experimental study of RTS surface change at Reτ ≃ 8800, considering the first measurement point at y+ = 88. Antonia and Luxton [495] and Hanson and Ganapathisubramani [511] studied RTS surface change at Reτ ≃ 1700 with performing the first measurement at y+ = 95. Jacobi and McKeon [508] conducted the measurements down to y+ = 3 for an RTS surface change at Reτ ≃ 970 − 1200. They assumed that the viscous sublayer departed from equilibrium. For high Reynolds number flows, the IEL can be extended to the larger y+. For example, Saito and Pullin [518] performed an wall-modelled LES study of RTS surface change with Reτ ≃ 2  × 104 − 2  × 106, considering the first grid at y+ = 410. Silva-Lopes et al. [515] conducted wall-modelled LES at Reτ ≃ 1.5  × 105 with the first grid point at y+ = 260. Rouhi et al. [522] conducted DNS studies of RTS and STR surface changes and showed that log-law assumption for the smooth patch is valid after a higher y+compared to that of rough patch. They found an error of approximately 5 % compared to experiments for velocity profile if the log-layer assumed positioned at y+ = 30. Ismail et al. [526] performed a DNS study of RTS surface change at Reτ = 920 with cube roughness and observed the characteristics of smooth wall below y+ = 50.

7.4.2. Internal boundary layer

One of the most important representatives of flow recovery after a surface change is the thickness of the IBL. Various definitions of the IBL have been proposed in the literature (Table 1 of Savelyev and Taylor [503]). In the majority of studies, the growth of δi with the streamwise location is described by δi = ∝xb with various values of b ranging from 0.2 to 0.8 proposed based on the adopted definition of IBL. Those studies that employed similar definitions have obtained close values of b. For example, Cheng and Castro [514] and Lee [525] employed the definition of Pendergrass and Arya [529] for an STR surface change at Reτ = 2500 and obtained close values of b (0.33 and 0.22). Antonia & Luxton [494] and Win et al. [530] used the definition of Antonia & Luxton [494] for a STR surface change at Reτ = 2200 and 2600, and achieved values of 0.72 and 0.8 for b respectively.
Li et al. [531] observed the recovery of the viscous region almost immediately to an equilibrium state with the new wall condition. Rouhi et al. [522] observed that the buffer region and beyond takes 5δ (over the smooth patch) and 2.5δ (over the rough patch) before recovering to equilibrium conditions. Ismail et al. [523] observed a slow recovery of mean flow and Reynolds stress profile. They divided the flow after an RTS surface change into two zones: (i) initial strong non-equilibrium zone (0 < x/δ < 0.5) with sharp change in skin friction proceeding a weak non-equilibrium zone (x/δ > 0.5). Ismail et al. [526] suggested a length of an order 50δ over the smooth surface after a RTS surface change to recover the Reynold stress. Van Buren et al. [532] studied flow recovery of turbulent flows after RTS surface change in pipes. They reported the recovery of pressure gradient, skin friction and mean streamwise momentum after approximately 20 radii downstream of the surface change, while the turbulent stresses is recovered after about 120 radii downstream of the surface change.
Rouhi et al. [524] conducted DNS of turbulent flow over RTS and STR step changes using a 3D sinusoidal surface (egg-carton), considering the roughness origin was placed aligned with (no-step), below (step-up) and above (step-down) the smooth patch. They studied the effect of the roughness height of ks+≃106−160, as well as a range of Reτ ≃ 650 − 700 over the rough patch and Reτ ≃ 400 − 450 over the smooth patch. They found that changing the roughness origin and Reτ significantly influence the departure from equilibrium, while the effect of the roughness height was marginal.
Although extensive studies have been conducted in this field, turbulent flow over roughness inhomogeneity is far from being understood. For example, limited type of roughness has been considered in the literature, and recording experiments for a wider range of roughness is required. No study has been performed with multiple patches of roughness, which can have a particular application in naturally formed biofouling on ship hulls. Although wall-modelled LES has shown promise in modelling these type of flows, a wide gap for developing numerical models for such flows exists. Almost all of the previous studies have concentrated on the flow characteristic of such flows without investigation of passive scalar transport that can significantly contribute to heat transfer applications and the study of air pollutant dispersion.

8. Conclusion

Turbulent flow over rough surfaces has been studied for about a century through a great deal of experimental and CFD studies. Roughness can influence fluid flow and heat transfer by increasing pressure drop, altering flow regime laminar-turbulent transition, and by inducing secondary flow motions which lead to an enhancement in flow mixing and heat transfer.
In most cases, roughness can be quantified by a single scaling parameter, known as equivalent sand-grain roughness height ks, which can be expressed based on the statistical parameters of surface roughness (Ra, sk, ku, ES, etc.). Empirical correlations for the calculation of ks were reviewed in this paper and it was found that methods using only a single parameter or height (Ra or Rq, etc.) were unsuccessful in modelling flows over rough surfaces. Therefore, a series of studies have included the effect of roughness density in the formulation of ks, and alternatively incorporating surface moments such as sk and ku owing to the difficulties in measuring the roughness density in irregular roughness. However, no universal correlation has been proposed so far. The selection of an appropriate correlation for ks is difficult due to the variety of the proposed correlations, which can vary up to a factor of 5 [5]. Other reasons are that ks is a roughness scale in the fully rough regime which is not necessarily useful in the transitionally rough regime, and the wide diversity of roughness types. In addition, the dense roughness regime, which is associated with d-type roughness, does not scale with ks. Therefore, as stated by Flack [286], it is time to move beyond characterising roughness by ks. Another roughness scale is required that can describe the onset of roughness effect and transition to the fully rough regime an well as the shape of roughness function in all roughness regimes.
Fluid flow models, particularly those that account for surface roughness, have been developed based on the structure of turbulent flows. Numerous experiments have been conducted, and several theories have been hypothesised to describe flow structure over smooth and rough surfaces. The Monin–Obukhov (M-O) similarity hypothesis was one of the initial theories that were proposed based on the mixing length theory to describe vertical distributions of mean flow velocities and temperature using “universal functions”. Experimental studies suggest that M-O similarity is about 10-20 % accurate and can merely be applied to the active region of turbulent flow [129]. On the other hand, Townsend hypothesis thoroughly explains large-scale motions near smooth in both inner and outer layers and provides a conceptual model of boundary layer kinetics and eddy motions. The wall similarity hypothesis is an extension of the Townsend's Reynolds number similarity to rough-wall flows, which has been verified by numerous experimental and DNS studies for various roughness regimes and flow conditions, including separated flows. Wall similarity explains that the effect of the roughness is confined in the roughness sublayer and the outer region remains unaffected by roughness. However, evidence of roughness effects into the outer layer has also been observed in several experiments where the ratio between the thickness of boundary layer and roughness height were smaller than 40 [81,235]. Conversely, some other researchers found similarity at lower ratios.
Despite progress in finding criteria for the transition from k-type to d-type roughness, a fully accurate distinction between roughness types has not been proposed so far. The proposed criteria include state of the vortex shedding, roughness solidity λ, and effective slope ES. The k-type roughness injects a vortex into the flow above the crest of the roughness elements (vortex shedding) which diffuses into the flow further away from the roughness crests. However, weak vortex shedding has also been observed in d-type roughness. Other studies have associated the k-type with sparse roughness regimes (λ < 0.15) and the d-type with dense roughness regimes (λ > 0.15). A number of recent studies have observed that at effective slopes ES ≈ 0.35, that is a delineation between waviness regime (ES < 0.35) and roughness regime (ES > 0.35), is associated with a solidity value of λ = 0.175, approximately close to the value λ = 0.15. The available data from various studies concerning turbulent flow over d-type and intermediate-type roughness does not point to an agreed conclusion or trend, which is mainly related to sheltering effect introduced by these types of roughness.
The distribution of mean velocity over rough surfaces can be characterised as a downward shift in mean velocity from the smooth case using a roughness function (ΔU+) which is solely a function of roughness scale ks+. However, correlating ΔU+ with the roughness scale is only valid for sparse roughness regime (k-type roughness). The dense roughness regime (d-type roughness) does not correlate with the roughness scale, whereas it can be scaled with the effective slope (ES). Recent studies suggested employing both roughness scale and effective slope to be able to universally scale turbulent flow in all roughness regimes.
In general, roughness can cause an early transition from laminar to turbulent through bypass transition. Although a significant body of study has cast light on the mechanisms of bypass laminar-turbulent transition due to isolated roughness, bypass transition caused by distributed roughness has not been fully understood. However, no apparent effect on the friction factor and the laminar-turbulent transition properties (critical Reynolds number) for relative roughness lower than 1% has been reported [379].
Numerous studies on turbulent flow over rough surfaces have been devoted to heterogeneous roughness which contributes to important engineering applications including heat transfer, ABL flows, aerodynamics, hydraulics, etc. Most studies have investigated streamwise inhomogeneities which cause a transition in the boundary layer, and spanwise inhomogeneities which contribute to the generation of secondary flow motions, while a few studies investigated a combination of both. Although recent experimental and DNS studies have shed light on the different aspects of flow recovery over spanwise surface changes, this area of research is not fully understood. Spanwise heterogeneity resulting from surface roughness have demonstrated the formation of the secondary flow of Prandtls second kind in the turbulent boundary layer. Many of the recent DNS studies have been devoted to investigating this type of secondary flow induced by roughness. The formation of secondary flow is related to the Reynolds stresses' inhomogeneities and leads to the thickening and thinning of boundary layer thickness in the cross-plane of the boundary layer. There is a wide research gap for investigating scalar transport over both spanwise and streamwise heterogeneous surfaces.
The main conclusion of this review paper is that despite many advances being made in respect to the fundamental understanding of turbulent flows over rough surfaces, this subject is far from being comprehensively understood. In almost every study or theory, supporting and conflicting evidence can be found. The main reason is related to the chaotic and random nature of turbulent flows that make accurate predictions almost unattainable. Other reasons are a lack of sufficient systematic studies on the structure of turbulent flow and because of the diverse variety of roughness which significantly impacts the dynamics of the flow in roughness sublayer.
Recent advances in additive manufacturing technology, have increased the possibility of fabricating artificial engineered roughness ranging in size from macro to nanoscale [54,112]. This technology provides the designer with the ability to control the shape and pattern of the roughness elements and can be used for the fabrication of roughness to perform systematic experiments. The significant computational power of modern computers and high-performance computing have provided the ability to perform DNS of turbulent flows over realistic roughness. This active area of research seems set for further investigation. Advances in these technologies coupled with a complete synthesised and thorough in-depth review of the domain area, as presented by this paper, can help bridge the knowledge gap in our fundamental understanding of turbulent flows over rough surfaces.
